146.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Wahdat-ul-Wujud — Unity of Being; Haq and Khalq are one
Wahdat-ush-Shuhud — Creator and creation are identical
Wahdat-ush-Shuhud — Doctrine associated with Ibn Arabi
146.x: Wahdat-ul-Wujud means Unity of Being and identifies Haq, the Creator, with Khalq, creation. Wahdat-ush-Shuhud means Unity of Appearance or Witness and holds that creation reflects God rather than being identical with Him.
146.tq: Distinguish the two doctrines by comparing identity with reflection.
xs: **Wahdat-ul-Wujud** = **"Unity of Being"**: **Haq** (Creator) and **Khalq** (creation) are one — option **(1)** is correct.
**Wahdat-ush-Shuhud** = **"Unity of Appearance/Witness"**: creation **only reflects God** — so options (2) and (3) swap the meanings.
Wahdat-ush-Shuhud belongs to **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi**, not **Ibn Arabi**.
xa: ⚠ **Wujud** = Being (Ibn Arabi, **Qadiri**, **Chishti**); **Shuhud** = Appearance (Sirhindi, **Naqshbandi**).
Sirhindi, the **Naqshbandi** saint, framed Wahdat-ush-Shuhud as his **counter-doctrine**.

146.s: With whom is the doctrine of Wahdat-ush-Shuhud associated?
146.x: Wahdat-ush-Shuhud (Unity of Appearance) was taught by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi; Wahdat-ul-Wujud is Ibn Arabi's.

146.s: What does the doctrine of Wahdat-ul-Wujud hold?
146.x: Wahdat-ul-Wujud (Unity of Being) holds that Haq and Khalq are one; the view that creation only reflects God is Wahdat-ush-Shuhud.

Sufis are well known for their practice of Sama, which involves reciting or singing devotional songs and poetry. This was done to evoke a state of spiritual ecstasy and divine love, for both themselves and their followers.

148.x: Sufism, like Bhakti, stressed loving devotion to one God over formal ritual, so its philosophy parallels Bhakti rather than karma, kalpa or gyana.

151.s: Blue Water Policy is associated with
151.x:
The Blue Water Policy (Política da Água Azul) was introduced by the Portuguese Viceroy Francisco de Almeida, the first Portuguese Viceroy in India. The main objective of this policy was to establish Portuguese naval supremacy in the Indian Ocean rather than acquiring extensive inland territories. Almeida believed that control over the sea routes would enable Portugal to dominate the lucrative spice trade between Europe and Asia. To implement this policy, the Portuguese developed a strong navy, built coastal forts and attempted to eliminate Arab and other European competitors from maritime trade. Although Almeida emphasized naval supremacy, his successor Afonso de Albuquerque shifted Portuguese policy towards territorial expansion by capturing Goa, Malacca and Hormuz. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Blue Water Policy – Francisco de Almeida
• Successor – Afonso de Albuquerque
• Aim – Control of Indian Ocean trade

151.x: William Hawkins sailed from the East India Company’s ship and reached to Surat in 1608 A.D. from Hector. After initial resistance from Portuguese, Hawkins arrived at the Mughal Court of Jahangir in Agra in April, 1609 A.D. Hawkins arrived at the Mughal Court with a letter signed by King James I of England, having introduction about Hawkins and the request of Mughal emperor’s favourable treatment for British traders. Therefore, Hawkins mission was a combination fo both, an imperial embassy and a commercial endeavour. He was sent by company, but with the credentials from the King, which made him representative of both– the King and the company, in the eyes of Mughal court. Hawkins was a good speaker of Turkish language. Jahangir was impressed by his knowledge of Turkish language and bestowed Hawkins, with the title of ‘English Khan’. Jahangir also granted Hawkins a mansab of 400. Therefore, statement (I) is false and the statement (II) is true.

156.s: Who translated the Bible into Telugu for the first time?
156.x:
Benjamin Schulz (Schultze) was the first missionary to translate the Bible into Telugu during 1746–47. He mastered the Telugu language and translated the Bible to make Christian teachings accessible to Telugu-speaking people. His work also contributed to the development of modern Telugu prose and printing. Besides the Bible, he prepared linguistic works that helped European scholars learn Telugu. His translation occupies an important place in the history of Telugu literature and missionary activity in South India. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• First Telugu Bible Translator – Benjamin Schulz
• Period – 1746–47

156.s: Who translated the Bible into Telugu in 1746–47?
156.x:
Benjamin Schulz (Benjamin Schultze), a German Lutheran missionary associated with the Danish-Halle Mission, was the first person to translate the Bible into Telugu during 1746–47. Recognizing the need to communicate Christian teachings in the local language, he mastered Telugu and undertook the translation of the Bible. His work became a landmark in the history of Telugu prose and printing. The translation also contributed to the development of modern Telugu literature by introducing prose style and encouraging the publication of printed books. Benjamin Schulz's contribution extended beyond religious literature. He also prepared Telugu grammars and dictionaries, helping European scholars understand the Telugu language. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• First Telugu Bible Translator – Benjamin Schulz
• Period – 1746–47
• Contribution – Early Telugu prose and Christian literature

157.s: Which European power first established a factory at Machilipatnam?
157.x:
The Portuguese were the first Europeans to establish commercial contacts and a trading factory at Machilipatnam. They reached the Coromandel Coast soon after the discovery of the sea route to India by Vasco da Gama in 1498. Later, the Dutch, English and French also established trading factories at Machilipatnam because of its thriving textile trade and strategic location on the east coast. Machilipatnam subsequently became one of the busiest ports on the Coromandel Coast and an important centre for international trade. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• First European traders at Machilipatnam – Portuguese
• Later – Dutch, English and French

157.s: Where did the English establish their first factory in Coastal Andhra?
157.x:
Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam) was the first trading factory established by the English East India Company in Coastal Andhra in 1611. It was one of the busiest ports on the Coromandel Coast and served as an important centre for the export of textiles, indigo and spices. The English obtained permission from the Qutb Shahi rulers of Golconda to establish this factory. From Machilipatnam, the Company gradually expanded its commercial activities to other parts of South India, eventually laying the foundation for British political dominance. The port remained an important centre of international trade for the English, Dutch and French throughout the seventeenth century. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• First English Factory in Andhra – Machilipatnam (1611)
• Permission granted by – Qutb Shahi rulers
• Major Export – Cotton textiles

159.s: Carnatic War was fought between :
159.x: The First Carnatic War (1746-48 A.D.) was an offshoot of the Anglo-French rivalry in the Austrian War of succession that took place in Europe in 1740 AD. The British Commodore Bernett captured some French ships which became the immediate cause of the war. Nawab Anwaruddin sent an army under the command of Mahfooz Khan to besiege the French in Madras during the first Carnatic War. The French Army (under the command of Captain Paradise) defeated Nawab’s Army at the Battle of St. Thome near Adyar river. Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (18 Oct, 1748 A.D.) ended the War of Austrian succession and with it first Carnatic War ended and the Britishers reoccupied Madras. The first Carnatic War is memorable for the War of St. Thome.

He defeated Lally at Wandiwash and remained in Pondicherry.
He was an English commander who captured Madras in 1746.
He kept Salabat Jang in power at Hyderabad and won the Northern Circars in 1753.
162.x: Bussy supported Salabat Jang at Hyderabad and secured the Northern Circars for the French in 1753. He was later captured at Wandiwash.
162.tq: Combine the official’s political and territorial roles while rejecting swapped identities.
xs: **Bussy** kept **Salabat Jang** in power at Hyderabad and won the **Northern Circars (1753)** — option **(4)**.
He was **French**, not English, and was **captured at Wandiwash** — he did not defeat Lally.
**Madras (1746)** was taken by **La Bourdonnais**'s fleet.
xa: Bussy won at **Tumnapalem (1756)** with **Vijayaramaraju** of Vizianagaram → **Treaty of Charmahal**.
A French failure: Lally **pulled Bussy out of Hyderabad**.

162.s: Which of the following events is associated with Count de Lally?
o: Defeat of Anwaruddin at St. Thome
Capture of Fort St. David in 1758 and surrender of Pondicherry in 1761
162.x: Count de Lally, the French commander and Governor in the Third Carnatic War, captured Fort St. David in 1758 and surrendered Pondicherry on 16 January 1761.
162.tq: Link a commander with two events from the same war and reject swapped deeds.
xs: **Count de Lally** took **Fort St. David (1758)** and **surrendered Pondicherry** (**16 Jan 1761**) — option **(4)**.
**Machilipatnam (1759)** was taken by **Forde**; **St. Thome** was won by **Paradis**; **Madras (1746)** by **La Bourdonnais**.
xa: Count de Lally = **Third** Carnatic War (**APPSC-GS 2019**); defeated at Wandiwash (**UKPSC 2016**).
Lally **quarrelled with officials**; his **troops went unpaid**.

162.s: Which defeat showed the English naval advantage in the Carnatic struggles?
162.x: The English navy defeated d’Aché’s fleet off Pondicherry (1759), after which he withdrew to Mauritius.
162.tq: Distinguish naval action from land battles by identifying the fleet commander.
xs: The English navy beat **d'Aché's fleet off Pondicherry (1759)** — option **(2)**.
d'Aché then **withdrew to Mauritius**.
**Chendurthi**, **Wandiwash** and **St. Thome** were **land** battles.
xa: **Pocock** was the English admiral; he beat d'Ache in the **Bay of Bengal**.
Other reasons: **Bengal's resources after Plassey (1757)** and **better commanders** (Clive, Lawrence, Coote).

162.s: Which English commander, along with Clive, besieged Tiruchirappalli in the Second Carnatic War, forcing the French commander Law to surrender?
162.x: Stringer Lawrence with Clive besieged Tiruchirappalli, where the French commander Law surrendered.
162.tq: one-liner

162.s: On which date did Count de Lally surrender Pondicherry to the English?
162.x: Lally surrendered Pondicherry on 16 January 1761; 22 January 1760 is the date of Wandiwash.

162.s: Which ruler of Hyderabad, kept in power by Bussy, granted the Northern Circars to the French in 1753?
162.x: Bussy kept Salabat Jang in power at Hyderabad and in return won the Northern Circars for the French in 1753.

162.s: Who led the French force that defeated the Nawab of the Carnatic's army at St. Thome (Adyar) in 1746?
162.x: Captain Paradis with about 930 French troops beat Anwaruddin's army under Mahfuz Khan at St. Thome/Adyar.

162.s: Which French commander was taken prisoner at the Battle of Wandiwash?
162.x: Bussy, who had held Hyderabad for the French, was captured at Wandiwash (1760).

162.s: The famous Battle of Wandiwash in 1760 was fought by the British against whom?
162.x: Battle of Ambur (August, 1749 A.D.):- The combined armies of Muzaffar Jung, Chanda Sahib and the French defeated and Killed Anwar-ud-din at the Battle of Ambur near Bellore in August, 1749. Muzaffar Jung became the Subedar of Deccan. Duplex was appointed Governor of all the Mughal territories south of the river Krishna. The Nizam surrendered some districts in the Northern Circars to the French. A French army under Bussy was stationed in Hyderabad. Battle of Plassey (June, 1757 A.D.):- Fought between Nawab of Bengal Sirajuddaula and the British Army. Bengal was in control of the British after Plassey. Mir Jafar was placed on the throne by Robert Clive. In exchange, Mir Jafar ceded an area of the south of Calcutta known as 24 Pargana to the British for their services and gifted 2,34,000 pounds to Clive as personal gift reward. Battle of Wandiwash (January, 1760 A.D.) :- It occurred between French and British. French were defeated by the British. Sir Eyre Coote was the leader of the British Army while French troops were led by Count de Lally. Battle of Buxar (October, 1764 A.D.) :- Fought between allied forces of Mir Qasim, Shujauddaula, Shah Alam II and the British. British led by Hector Munro defeated the allied forces badly. Thus, option (b) will be the correct answer.

162.s: Over whom did Clive win the battles of Arni and Kaveripak?
162.x: During the Second Carnatic War, Clive defeated Raja Sahib and Chanda Sahib at Arni and Kaveripak in 1751–52.
162.tq: Identify the opposing commanders associated with a pair of battles.
xs: At **Arni and Kaveripak** (**1751-52**) Clive beat **Raja Sahib and Chanda Sahib** — option **(4)**.
**Conflans** was beaten at **Chendurthi**; **Lally** at **Wandiwash**.
xa: This followed Clive's **siege of Arcot (1751)**.
**Stringer Lawrence** and Clive then forced **Law** to surrender at **Tiruchirappalli**.

162.s: In which year was the Battle of Wandiwash fought on 22 January?
162.x: Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760; Chendurthi on 7 December 1758, Ambur in 1749 and Arcot in 1751.
xa: Ambur and Arcot belong to the **Second** war; Chendurthi and Wandiwash to the **Third**.
**St. Thome / Adyar (1746)** was the **First** war's battle.

162.s: Whose army of about 10,000 men was defeated by about 930 French troops at the Battle of St. Thome (Adyar) in 1746?
162.x: At St. Thome/Adyar (1746) about 930 French troops beat about 10,000 of the Nawab's men.
xa: The French were led by **Captain Paradis**; the Nawab's army by **Mahfuz Khan**.
Lesson: **disciplined European infantry** beat **much larger Indian armies**.

162.s: In which battle of 1749 was Nawab Anwaruddin of the Carnatic killed?
162.x: At Ambur (August 1749), the French with Muzaffar Jang and Chanda Sahib won, and Anwaruddin was killed.
162.tq: one-liner

162.s: Robert Clive held Arcot in 1751 with about 210 men for how many days?
162.x: Clive held Arcot for 53 days (23 September–14 November 1751) with about 210 men.
162.tq: one-liner

162.s: Who commanded the English army that won the Battle of Wandiwash (1760)?
162.x: Sir Eyre Coote beat Count de Lally at Wandiwash on 22 January 1760; Bussy was taken prisoner.

162.s: The French failed to establish power in the Deccan because:
o: Duplex was not a capable general
The English had a strong army
The French were not liked by the Indians
Pondicherry was not a strategic centre
162.x: One major cause of French failure in India was their weak naval strength. According to Voltaire, during the war of Austrian succession, the French naval strength was reduced so badly that the Navy had hardly any battleship left in the Seven Years War. On the other hand, the British had a strong naval force.

162.s: Which one among the following was a reason for which the French could not succeed in India in the 18th century?
o: They sided with the weak Indian sides such as Chanda Sahib and Muzaffar Jung.
Dupleix was called back at a crucial time.
They conspired against the Indian powers.
Their trading company was heavily dependent on the French Government.
162.x: The French company was state-controlled and dependent on the government, unlike the private, profit-driven English company, which hampered French success. The other options are not the reason given in the notes.

162.s: Which of the following was NOT a reason for the English success over the French in the Carnatic struggles?
o: Better English commanders such as Clive, Lawrence and Coote
Resources obtained from Bengal after Plassey
The French company was a private body run mainly for profit
162.x: The French company was controlled by the state, whereas the English company was a private body run for profit. The other options were reasons for English success.
162.tq: Find the reversed comparison in an explanation of comparative success.
xs: "The **French** company was a **private body run for profit**" is NOT a reason — option **(4)**.
In fact the **English** company was the **private body run for profit**; the French was **state-controlled**.
Real reasons: **naval superiority**, **Bengal's resources after Plassey (1757)**, **better commanders** (Clive, Lawrence, Coote).
xa: French failures: **Dupleix recalled**; Lally **quarrelled**; **troops unpaid**.
The French also **failed at Madras + Thanjavur**.

162.s: Which one of the following combinations represents French failures that weakened their position in India?
o: Recall of Dupleix, unpaid troops under Lally and withdrawal of Bussy from Hyderabad
Capture of Chandannagar, victory at Wandiwash and support for Muhammad Ali
Naval superiority, Bengal revenues and better English commanders
Victory at Chendurthi, capture of Machilipatnam and retention of Hyderabad
162.x: French difficulties included the recall of Dupleix, Lally’s quarrels and unpaid troops, failures at Madras and Thanjavur, and the withdrawal of Bussy from Hyderabad.
162.tq: Select the option containing only failures of one side.
xs: **Dupleix's recall**, **Lally's unpaid troops** and **Bussy's withdrawal from Hyderabad** were French failures — option **(1)**.
Option (3) lists **English** strengths; options (2) and (4) list **English** gains (Chandannagar, Wandiwash, Chendurthi, Machilipatnam).
xa: Lally also **quarrelled with officials** and **failed at Madras + Thanjavur**.
The French company was **state-controlled**.

162.s:
Consider the following statements about the Anglo-French rivalry:
1. The English East India Company was a private body run for profit.
2. The French East India Company was state-controlled.
3. The resources of Bengal after Plassey paid for the English wars in the south.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
162.x: All three are true: the English company was private, the French state-controlled, and Bengal's resources after 1757 funded the southern wars.

162.s: Why is Chendurthi known as the 'Plassey of Andhra'?
o: drove the French out of the Northern Circars
established French control over all the Northern Circars
162.x: Chendurthi, fought in 1758, has been called the ‘Plassey of Andhra’ because it drove the French out of the Northern Circars.
162.tq: Connect a famous comparative title with the specific political consequence of the battle.
xs: Chendurthi **drove the French out of the Northern Circars** — hence "**Plassey of Andhra**" (Malleson) — option **(2)**.
**Pondicherry** surrendered in **1761** after Wandiwash, not after Chendurthi.
xa: **Forde** and the **Vizianagaram army** beat **Conflans** on **7 Dec 1758**.
Forde then took **Machilipatnam (1759)**.

162.s: With regard to the establishment of French factories in India, which of the following is correctly matched?
162.x: The first French factory was established at Surat in 1668. The second was established at Masulipatnam in 1669 under a patent from the Sultan of Golconda.
162.tq: Start from the sure factory-date pair and eliminate the swapped location or year.
xs: **First French factory — Surat, 1668** is correct — option **(3)**.
The **second** was **Masulipatnam (1669)**, so options (1) and (2) swap them.
**Yanam** was French from **1723**, not a factory of **1753**.
xa: Masulipatnam's factory came under a patent from the **Sultan of Golconda**.
⚠ **Surat (1668)** first, **Masulipatnam (1669)** second.

162.s: What is the present status of Yanam, a former French settlement?
o: an enclave in Andhra Pradesh's Godavari delta administered as part of the Union Territory of Puducherry
a district of Andhra Pradesh created after 1954
a part of Tamil Nadu adjoining Karaikal
162.x: Yanam, French from 1723, is an enclave inside AP's Godavari delta but is administered as part of Puducherry UT. It is not an AP district, it is not in Tamil Nadu (Karaikal is), and Pondicherry's settlements passed to India in 1954.
162.tq: Yanam = in AP's Godavari delta, part of Puducherry UT
xs: **Yanam** is an enclave inside AP's **Godavari** delta, administered as part of **Puducherry** UT — option **(1)**.
It is not an AP district and not in Tamil Nadu; French territory passed to India from **1954**.
xa: Yanam was French **from 1723**.
AP angle: **Yanam** still part of Puducherry UT.
Pondicherry became a UT by the **14th Amendment (1962)**.

162.s: In which year did Bussy win the Northern Circars for the French?
162.x: Bussy won the Northern Circars for the French in 1753; they were lost after Chendurthi (1758) and the fall of Machilipatnam (1759).

162.s: From whom did the French get the patent for their second factory at Masulipatnam (1669)?
162.x: Masulipatnam was the second French factory (1669), set up on a patent from the Sultan of Golconda.

162.s: With whom did Bussy conclude the Treaty of Charmahal after the Battle of Tumnapalem (1756)?
162.x: Bussy won at Tumnapalem with Vijayaramaraju of Vizianagaram, which led to the Treaty of Charmahal.

162.x: Malleson called Chendurthi (1758) the "Plassey of Andhra" as it drove the French out of the Northern Circars.

162.x: Karaikal is in Tamil Nadu; Yanam is in the Godavari delta of AP, Mahe in Kerala and Chandernagore in Bengal.

162.x: Pondicherry was renamed Puducherry in 2006, not 1987; it became a UT by the 14th Amendment (1962).

162.s: After which battle of 1758, won by Colonel Forde, did the French lose the Northern Circars to the English?
162.x: Forde beat the French under Conflans at Chendurthi (1758) and took Machilipatnam in 1759, ending French control of the Northern Circars.

Match the following.
List I
List II

A. First Carnatic War

162.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Pondicherry was transferred to India in 1954.
2. Pondicherry became a Union Territory under the Fourteenth Amendment.
3. Pondicherry was renamed Puducherry in 1987.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
162.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Pondicherry was renamed Puducherry in 2006, not 1987.

xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: Pondicherry was **handed over in 1954**.
Statement 2: it became a UT by the **14th Amendment (1962)**.
Statement 3 wrong: it was renamed **Puducherry** in **2006**, not 1987.

163.s: Royal palace consisting of thousand pillars was constructed by the following ruler
Who was the last Subahdar (Governor) of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor?
163.x: Murshid Quli Khan, Nawab from 1717 and founder of the autonomous Bengal Nawabi, was the last Subahdar of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor. Shuja-ud-din, Alivardi Khan (who seized the throne by killing Sarfaraz) and Siraj-ud-Daula came later.
xs: **Murshid Quli Khan** was the **last Subahdar/Governor of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor** — option **(3)**.
Asked in **UPPSC 2013 and 2021**.
**Alivardi Khan** seized the throne by **killing Sarfaraz**; **Shuja-ud-din** and **Siraj-ud-Daula** came later.
xa: Murshid Quli became **Nawab of Bengal in 1717** and founded the **autonomous Bengal Nawabi**.
By **1735** Shuja-ud-din was "**too absolute to regard any orders from court**".

163.s: Who ruled Bengal immediately before Siraj-ud-Daula?
163.x: The order was Shuja-ud-din, Sarfaraz Khan, Alivardi Khan and Siraj-ud-Daula.
xa: All followed **Murshid Quli Khan (1717-27)**.
**Alivardi** seized the throne by **killing Sarfaraz**.
**Siraj-ud-Daula** was Alivardi's **grandson** and lost **Plassey**.

163.s: Which Nawab of Bengal was the son-in-law of Murshid Quli Khan?
163.x: Shuja-ud-din was the son-in-law of Murshid Quli Khan. Sarfaraz Khan was Shuja-ud-din’s son and Murshid Quli Khan’s grandson.
163.tq: Use family relationships to distinguish the two successive Nawabs connected with Murshid Quli Khan.
xs: **Shuja-ud-din** was the **son-in-law of Murshid Quli Khan** — option **(4)**.
**Sarfaraz Khan** was **Shuja-ud-din's son** (Murshid Quli's **grandson**).
**Siraj-ud-Daula** was the **grandson of Alivardi Khan**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes call **Sarfaraz** the "son of Murshid Quli Khan" — wrong.
Shuja-ud-din ruled **1727-39**.

163.s: Whose grandson was Siraj-ud-Daula?
163.x: Alivardi Khan, earlier Deputy Governor of Bihar, was succeeded by his grandson Siraj-ud-Daula.
xa: Alivardi seized the throne by **killing Sarfaraz** (**1740**).

163.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Siraj-ud-Daula — Last independent Nawab of Bengal
Robert Clive — Founder of the British Empire in India
Mir Jafar — Founder of the autonomous Bengal Nawabi
163.x: Mir Jafar was the puppet Nawab installed after Plassey. The autonomous Bengal Nawabi was founded by Murshid Quli Khan.
163.tq: Find the swapped title by matching each person with the precise designation associated with him.
xs: "**Mir Jafar — founder of the autonomous Bengal Nawabi**" is NOT correctly matched — option **(4)**.
Mir Jafar was the **puppet Nawab installed after Plassey**; the founder was **Murshid Quli Khan**.
Correct: **Siraj-ud-Daula** — last independent Nawab; **Clive** — founder of the British Empire; **Jagat Seth** — "world banker".
xa: Clive as **Founder of the British Empire in India**: **APPSC 2019**, **BPSC 2020**.
**Jagat Seth** was Bengal's great **banking house**.

163.s: Of which province was Alivardi Khan the Deputy Governor before he became Nawab of Bengal?
163.x: Alivardi Khan was earlier Deputy Governor of Bihar; he took the throne by killing Sarfaraz Khan at Giria (1740).

163.s: Whose son was Sarfaraz Khan, Nawab of Bengal?
163.x: Sarfaraz was the son of Shuja-ud-din (and grandson of Murshid Quli Khan), not Murshid Quli's son.

163.s: In which battle of 1740 did Alivardi Khan kill Sarfaraz Khan and take the throne of Bengal?
163.x: Alivardi Khan defeated and killed Sarfaraz Khan at Giria in 1740 and became Nawab of Bengal.

163.s: Which of the following was the last Subedar (Governor) of Bengal to be appointed by Mughal Emperor?
163.x: Murshid Quli Khan was the last Subahdar of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor; later Nawabs such as Shuja-ud-din acted independently, so the other options are wrong.

163.s: What was the main result of the English misuse of dastaks?
o: Transfer of Calcutta to the French
Recognition of Mir Jafar as Subahdar
Loss of revenue to the Nawab
163.x: The 1717 farman allowed duty-free Company trade, but Company servants misused dastaks for private trade, causing the Nawab to lose revenue.
163.tq: Connect the misuse of a fiscal privilege with its direct administrative consequence.
xs: The misuse of **dastaks** caused a **loss of revenue to the Nawab** — option **(4)**.
**Company servants** used dastaks for **private trade**.
xa: The **Farman of 1717 (Farrukhsiyar)** gave **duty-free trade**.
Misuse of the farman was a cause of conflict with **Siraj-ud-Daula**.

163.s: Murshid Quli Khan is associated with which one of the following administrative changes in Bengal?
o: Shifting the capital from Dacca to Murshidabad
Shifting the capital from Murshidabad to Dacca
Shifting the capital from Calcutta to Dacca
Shifting the capital from Patna to Murshidabad
163.x: Murshid Quli Khan shifted the capital of Bengal from Dacca to Murshidabad.
163.tq: Test the location change directly by distinguishing the old capital from the new one.
xs: **Murshid Quli Khan** shifted the capital from **Dacca to Murshidabad** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the direction of the shift.
xa: He rose from **Diwan** → **Subahdar** → **Nawab of Bengal in 1717**, founding the **autonomous Bengal Nawabi**.
He was the **last Subahdar of Bengal appointed by the Mughal Emperor** (UPPSC 2013, 2021).
Revenue: **ijaradari** (revenue farming) and conversion of jagir land into **khalisa**.

163.s: What does the term 'ijaradari' in the revenue administration of Bengal refer to?
o: Collection of land revenue through contractors
Collection of customs duties only from European companies
Direct collection of revenue by village headmen
Assignment of jagirs exclusively to Mughal princes
163.x: Ijaradari was revenue farming: contractors called ijaradars collected the land revenue (APPSC 2018), the contract-based collection also called mal jasmani under Murshid Quli Khan.
163.tq: Discriminate between a revenue-collection method and unrelated forms of land assignment or customs collection.
xs: **Ijaradari** (revenue farming) meant **contractors (ijaradars) collected land revenue** — option **(1)**.
This was asked in **APPSC 2018**.
xa: The contract-based revenue collection was called **mal jasmani**.
Murshid Quli converted **jagir land** into **khalisa** (crown land).
⚠ Don't confuse with **dastaks** — trade passes misused by Company servants for private trade.

163.s: What was the principal significance of converting jagir land into khalisa under Murshid Quli Khan?
o: It transferred the land permanently to the English Company
It converted the land into private property of the zamindars
It exempted the land from all forms of revenue
It placed the land under direct state revenue administration
163.x: Conversion of jagir land into khalisa brought the land under direct state control for revenue purposes.
163.tq: Apply the distinction between assigned jagir land and directly administered khalisa land.
xs: Converting jagir land into **khalisa** made it **crown land** under direct state revenue — option **(4)**.
It did not go to the English or to zamindars, nor was it exempt from revenue.
xa: Revenue on such land was collected by **ijaradars** (revenue farming, APPSC 2018).
The contract-based collection = **mal jasmani**.

163.s: By what other name was ijaradari, the contract-based revenue collection in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan, known?
163.x: Ijaradari, revenue farming through ijaradars, was also called mal jasmani.

163.s: In which year did Murshid Quli Khan become the Nawab of Bengal?
163.x: Murshid Quli Khan rose from Diwan to Subahdar and became Nawab of Bengal in 1717.

164.s: Who was the Nawab of Bengal when the Battle of Buxar was fought?
164.x: On 22/23 October, 1764 A.D. British Army defeated allied forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Oudh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. British Army’s command was in the hands of Major Hector Munro in the Battle of Buxar. The battle of Buxar assured the result of Plassey battle and established British supremacy on Banaras and Allahabad (Prayagraj) across the Ganges. The battle of Buxar made way for British and proved that there was no strong competitor before the British. The battle of Buxar completed what Plassey had begun. During the battle of Buxar Nawab of Bengal was Mir Jafar. According to Sir James Stephen, ‘’The battle of Buxar deserves more credit than the battle of Plassey as the origin of British power in India”. If the results of both significant battles are analyzed, it can be said that the battle of Plassey was won by treachery, but the battle of Buxar showed the supremacy of English armies and military skills. Plassey made the English the only controllers of Bengal while Buxar raised the political prestige of the Company throughout India.

It is clearly characterised as a historical novel set against the backdrop of the Pathan–Mughal conflicts during Akbar's reign. His notable works, including Anandamath (1882), Kapalkundala (1866), and Devi Chaudhurani (1884), reflect the social, cultural, and moral concerns of a colonised society striving for self-identity. 166.s: Englishmen made the Treaty of Srirangapatna with–
166.x: Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92 A.D.) ended with the Treaty of Srirangapatna (1792 A.D.). The treaty of Seringapatam (Srirangapatna) was signed in March 1792 A.D. between Tipu Sultan of Mysore and Lord Cornwallis on behalf of British East India Company. The agreement also included representative of the Nizam of Hyderabad and Maratha Empire, requiring Tipu to Cede half of his Kingdom. According to the treaty, Half of the territories of Tipu were snatched away from him and divided among Marathas, British, and Nizam. Tipu had to pay Rs. 330 lakhs as war indemnity to British as his two sons were kept hostage. These was a terms and condition in the treaty that until Tipu wouldn’t provide 3 crore rupees, his two sons will be under British protection.

167.s: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
o: To maintain a large standing army at others expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a fixed income for the Company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States
167.x: Statement (c) does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance: The primary objective was to establish military and political dominance rather than ensuring a stable revenue for the Company. Though the Subsidiary Alliance system was quite old, Wellesley gave it a definite shape. Under the system, the ruler of the allied Indian state was compelled to accept the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. The ruler, unable to pay the expenses, had to cede a part of his kingdom to the British. The British agreed to defend the ruler from his enemies. They also controlled the defence and foreign relations of the protected ally. In return, the Indian ruler of the protected state should keep a British Resident at his court and disband his own army.  Indian rulers should not employ Europeans in their service without the approval of the British.  Indian rulers should not negotiate with any other Indian ruler without consulting the Governor-General. • The System of Subsidiary Alliance was also aimed at preventing French influence (the Napoleonic threat) from entering India. This system enabled the British to uphold a substantial army, with the financial burden falling Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 154 on the local rulers (it helped the British to have paramountcy over the Indian States), and was not implemented for securing a fixed income for the East India Company.

167.x: Governor-General Lord Wellesley came to India in 1798 A.D. at a time when the British were locked in a life and death struggle with France all over the world. The fear of Napoleon haunted the Britishers everywhere. To achieve his political aims, Wellesley relied on the system of Subsidiary Alliance. While the practice of helping Indian rulers with a paid British force was quite old, it was given shape by Wellesley who used it to sub-ordinate the Indian states to the paramountcy of the company. Under the subsidiary Alliance system, the ruler of the allying state was compelled to accept the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. However, to secure a fixed income for the company was not under the agenda of the Subsidiary Alliance.

167.s: The Subsidiary Alliance was not accepted by-
167.x: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) cleverly used a subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First Subsidiary Alliance was signed in 1765 with Awadh where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Awadh on a fixed payment to the Company. 167.s: Which Governor-General is associated with the ' Doctrine of Lapse '?
167.x: Dalhousie Lord Dalhousie is closely associated with the Doctrine of Lapse, a policy under which the British annexed princely states whose rulers died without a natural male heir, disallowing adopted heirs from succession. This policy led to the annexation of several states, including Satara, Jhansi, and Nagpur. It significantly contributed to resentment that fuelled the Revolt of 1857.

Blue Water Policy aimed at Portuguese trade supremacy in the Indian Ocean. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #91 · pp 173-174]

167.s: Awadh served as a classic buffer state because it

167.s: Under which policy was the expression "breakwaters to the storm" used for the princes?

Subordinate union came through the **Crown** (**Queen's Proclamation**): annexation stopped, the **right of adoption** was recognised and borders were guaranteed.
**Doctrine of Lapse** was **Dalhousie's** (1848) and **Ring-fence** was **Warren Hastings'** — both belong to the Company era, before 1858.
xa: Policy sequence: **Ring-fence** (Warren Hastings) → **Subsidiary Alliance** (Wellesley, **1798**) → **Subordinate isolation** (Lord Hastings, **1813-23**) → **Doctrine of Lapse** (Dalhousie, **1848**) → **Subordinate union** (Crown, after 1858).
Lapse annexations and the Awadh takeover turned rulers, **taluqdars** and sepoys against the Company → policy abandoned after **1857**.

168.s:
Statement (A): Moturpha is a salt tax levied by the British East India Company.
Statement (B): The revenue collected by the British East India Company from the Zamindars is called Peshcush.
168.x:
Statement (A) is false. Moturpha was not a salt tax. It was a professional or trade tax imposed on artisans, craftsmen, traders and occupational groups by the British East India Company. The salt tax was a separate levy imposed on the manufacture and sale of salt.
Statement (B) is true. Peshcush refers to the fixed annual tribute or land revenue paid by Zamindars to the British East India Company under the Zamindari system. It became an important source of revenue during British rule in the Madras Presidency. Therefore, Statement (A) is false and Statement (B) is true. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Moturpha – Tax on professions, trades and occupations.
• Peshcush – Fixed revenue paid by Zamindars to the British.

168.s: What does "Moturpha" refer to?
168.x:
Moturpha was a professional tax imposed on artisans and craftsmen, particularly on weavers and their looms. It was one of the important taxes collected during the colonial period and was strongly opposed by the weaving community because it increased their economic burden. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Moturpha – Tax on Looms

168.s: Moturpha indicates:
168.x: Moturpha was a tax on looms, a trade/profession tax on weavers and artisans. It was not a toddy, sugar or salt tax.

168.s: Statement (A): Moturpha is a salt tax levied by British East India Company. Statement (B): The revenue collected by the British East India Company from the zamindars was called ' Peshcush '.
168.x: Moturpha was a profession or trade tax on artisans, weavers and traders, not a salt tax-so Statement A is false. ' Peshcush ' correctly refers to the fixed tribute that zamindars and other intermediary revenue-holders paid to the East India Company under the Permanent Settlement, making Statement B true. Distinguishing colonial revenue terms is a frequently tested area.

168.s: Which of the following was a major consequence associated with the Ryotwari system in the Andhra region?
o: Abolition of direct contact between cultivator and government

Ryotwari was settled with the **ryot directly** — it did not abolish that contact or work through zamindars.
xa: First region: **Baramahal (1792)** under **Captain Alexander Read** with **Munro**.

168.s: Which of the following correctly represents the regional distribution of Zamindari and Ryotwari in Andhra?

Zamindari in Rayalaseema and Ryotwari in the Northern Circars

169.x:
Sir Shonthi Venkataramamurthy, one of the distinguished irrigation engineers of Andhra, strongly advocated the construction of a major irrigation project across the Godavari River near Polavaram. He proposed that the project be named "Ramapada Sagaram." His proposal highlighted the enormous irrigation potential of the Godavari River and emphasized that its waters could transform the drought-prone regions of Andhra through irrigation, drinking water supply and hydroelectric generation. Although Sir Arthur Cotton pioneered irrigation development through the construction of the Dowleswaram Anicut, the proposal to build the Polavaram project as Ramapada Sagaram is associated with Sir Shonthi Venkataramamurthy. Later, Dr. K. L. Rao also supported the development of India's river valley projects and interlinking of rivers, but the original proposal carrying the name Ramapada Sagaram is credited to Sir Shonthi Venkataramamurthy. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).

170.s: Subsidiary Alliance was implemented during the reign of –
170.x: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) cleverly used a subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First Subsidiary Alliance was signed in 1765 with Awadh where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Awadh on a fixed payment to the Company. The evolved version of the Subsidiary Alliance was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad (1798 AD and 1800 AD), Mysore (1799 AD), Tanjore (1799 AD), Oudh (1801 AD), Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle of Barar (1803 AD), Sindhiya (1804 AD), Holkar (1818 AD), Jodhpur, Jaipur, Machheri, Bundi and Bharatpur. 172.s: Lord Lytton is not associated with which of the following?
172.x: Lord Lytton was an English politician who served as the Viceroy of India from 1876 to 1880. His tenure as Viceroy was marked by a controversial policy known as the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, which aimed to regulate the Indian vernacular press and limit its freedom of expression. The policies introduced included the Indian Arms Act of 1878, according to which, it was a criminal offence for Indians to carry arms without a license. The Act was discriminatory as it did not apply to the British, Anglo-Indians, Europeans, and certain government personnel. Famine Codes were given by the Famine Commission that was set up in 1878 under the Chairmanship of Sir Richard Strachey (Strachey Commission) during the tenure of Lord Lytton only. The infamous 'Famine Codes,' have been criticized for their handling of the 1876-1878 famine in India, which resulted in significant loss of life. Ilbert Bill on the other hand was introduced in 1883 by Lord Ripon that allowed Indian Judges and Magistrates to try British Offenders in criminal cases at the district level.

172.s: Who among the following introduced the Vernacular Press Act?
172.x: Lord Lytton (1876-1880 A.D.) passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878 A.D. The Ryotwari System was introduced in the Madras Presidency by Sir Thomas Munro during the early nineteenth century. Under this system, the government collected land revenue directly from individual cultivators (Ryots) instead of through Zamindars or intermediaries. Every ryot was recognized as the proprietor of his land, provided he regularly paid the land revenue fixed by the government. The system was first experimented with in parts of South India and later became the principal land revenue system in the Madras Presidency. It aimed to eliminate intermediaries, but in practice the heavy land tax often placed a severe burden on cultivators. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

This system was launched in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi (U.P.) etc. It is also known as Istimarari Maalguzari, Bishwedari etc. The Permanent Settlement stood on the following features - It recognized the landlords as the proprietors of the land. It also recognized the rights of a hereditary successor or lawful successors of the landlords. The government believed that these landlords would remain faithful to the British. The landlords were given the right to transfer or sell their land. All the rights of the landlords depended on their payment of the fixed revenue on the fixed date at the treasury of the government. All their rights ended if they failed to pay. This was one reason for increased litigation. An increase in intermediaries between farmers and landlords was another reason for increased litigation. The total amount of revenue to be paid by each landlord for his Zamindari was fixed once and for all. It was agreed that the tax rate would not increase in the future.

175.s: Who introduced the revenue policy in Rayalaseema?

175.s: Who was known as the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema?

175.s: Sir Thomas Munro is associated with the land revenue settlement:
175.x: Ryotwari System was the second system of collection of land revenue after Permanent Settlement. Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read were the founders of this system. This system was first introduced in Baramahal district (Tamil Nadu). After that, this system was introduced in Madras, Assam, Coorg and some areas of Bombay. In Ryotwari System, the ownership rights were transferred to the peasants. British government collected taxes directly from the peasants around 51% of British occupied Indian area was included in this system. The high rate of taxes and strictness during collection became a significant cause of struggle between money lenders and peasants.

175.s: Who suppressed the landlords of Rayalaseema?
175.x: Thomas Munro, as Collector of the Ceded districts in 1800, suppressed the Palegars with the help of General Campbell.

175.s: Where were Thomas Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts?

xs: Munro's HQ as first **Collector of the Ceded Districts (1800)** was **Anantapur** — option **(2)**.
**Pattikonda** (Kurnool) is where he died of cholera in **1827**.
xa: He was **Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts** from **1800-07** (some notes say 1802 for the start).
He was buried at **Gooty**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

xa: UPSC notes give his governorship as **1819-26**.
He was born **27 May 1761** in **Glasgow**.

175.s: Which of the following best represents Thomas Munro's administrative philosophy?
o: Exclusive reliance on village headmen and moneylenders
Direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries and communication in fluent Telugu
Permanent fixation of revenue irrespective of local conditions
Indirect rule through zamindars and complete absence of official contact with cultivators
175.x: Munro favoured direct contact with cultivators, avoided intermediaries and was fluent in Telugu. He was also particularly fond of Rayalaseema.
175.tq: Choose the option that combines the distinctive elements of a stated administrative philosophy.
xs: Munro stood for **direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries**, and spoke **fluent Telugu** — option **(2)**.
He **distrusted Palegars** and big intermediaries, so indirect rule through zamindars is the opposite.
xa: He worked **without interpreters**.
Rayalaseema was chosen because it had **no strong zamindars**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

Arrange the following events chronologically:
A. Implementation of Ryotwari settlement in Madras.

175.s: The Permanent Settlement introduced by Cornwallis in 1793 was implemented in Andhra in 1802 with which immediate effect?
o: The auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed
The zamindars were replaced by village headmen
Land revenue was remitted during every crop failure
All Zamindari estates were immediately abolished
175.x: In Andhra, Cornwallis's 1793 Act was implemented in 1802; it abolished the auction system and fixed the tax. Zamindari abolition occurred much later in 1948.
175.tq: Apply the general settlement policy to its Andhra implementation.
xs: When Cornwallis's **1793** settlement was implemented in Andhra in **1802**, **the auction system was abolished and the tax was fixed** — option **(1)**.
Zamindars were not replaced or abolished; abolition came only in **1948**.
There was **no famine remission** under British revenue systems.
xa: Agreements ran for **10** years; farmers were reduced to **tenants**.
Andhra effects: absentee landlordism, **sub-infeudation**, no investment in land.
Some notes give the Andhra split as **9/10** to government, **1/10** to the zamindar.

175.s: The sale of many old zamindari estates under the Permanent Settlement led to the rise of which class?
o: a new body of village karanams
a class of hereditary ryot proprietors in Madras
a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders
a class of Palegar intermediaries in Rayalaseema
175.x: Many old zamindars lost their estates for arrears, which were purchased by urban merchants and moneylenders, creating a new landed class.
175.tq: Trace the ownership change caused by arrears and auction sales.
xs: Estate sales created **a new landed class of urban merchants and moneylenders** — option **(3)**.
Many old zamindars lost estates for **arrears** under the Sunset Law.
xa: Zamindari areas → **merchant-landlords**; ryotwari and mahalwari areas → **moneylender-landlords**.
**Karanams** were village officers under the Collector in Ryotwari — not a new class.
**Palegars** were suppressed by **Munro**, not created.

175.s: What did the zamindars of Coastal Andhra pay to the Company?
175.x: Coastal lands were divided into Haveli (direct Company control) and Zamindari areas, whose zamindars paid peshkash.
xa: Old estates of **Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram** came under peshkash.
Mootahs were held like proprietary estates after **1802**; many fell into arrears.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** confirmed valid **inam** titles on a **quit-rent**.

175.s: In which year was the Madras Inam Commission, which checked titles to rent-free inam lands, constituted?
175.x: The Madras Inam Commission was constituted in 1858 to investigate rent-free inam titles.
xa: Valid titles were confirmed on payment of a **quit-rent**.
Full ryotwari conversion of estates came in **1948**.

175.s: Against which system was the criticism made that the State became the 'ultimate landlord'?
175.x: Critics held that under Ryotwari the state became the ultimate landlord and its revenue was as heavy as zamindari rent.
xa: Ryotwari revenue was often **50%+** of produce.
**Alice Thorner**: ryotwari **isolated farmers** from the government.

175.s: In which region of Andhra did Thomas Munro first introduce the Ryotwari system in 1802?
175.x: Munro brought Ryotwari to the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) in 1802; the Northern Circars were mainly zamindari.
xa: A **2018** PYQ stem gave the date as **1808**; the answer is still **Munro**.
From **1808** village-lease settlements replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts until restored around **1820**.

175.s: Who assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the Palegars in the Ceded Districts before the introduction of Ryotwari settlement?
175.x: Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer Campbell before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.
175.tq: Discriminate between persons associated with administration, resistance and nomenclature.
xs: Munro suppressed the Palegars with military officer **Campbell** — option **(2)**.
**Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** was a Kurnool Polygar who revolted in the **1840s**.
**Vijayarama Gajapati Raju** was the Vizianagaram zamindar defeated at **Padmanabham (1794)**.
**Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** proposed the name **Rayalaseema**.

Uyyalawada looted the treasury at **Kovela Kuntla**.

175.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt in the 1840s is associated with which incident?
o: Defeating the Vizianagaram zamindar at Padmanabham
Introducing the Mahalwari system in Nellore
Obtaining the Northern Circars through a Mughal farman
Looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla
175.x: During the Kurnool Polygar revolt in the 1840s, Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy looted the treasury at Kovela Kuntla.
175.tq: Link the rebel with the specific action and place.
xs: **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy**'s **1840s** revolt is linked to **looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla** — option **(4)**.
He was a **Kurnool Polygar**; Padmanabham (**1794**) was the Vizianagaram zamindar's defeat.
xa: Palegar resistance (**Uyyalawada**) followed **Munro**'s ryotwari in Rayalaseema.
Munro had suppressed about **80** palegars with **Campbell**.

175.s: After 1802, Haveli lands were grouped into mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars. As what did the mootahdars generally hold them?
175.x: After 1802, mootahs were auctioned to mootahdars, who held them in the manner of proprietary estates. Many mootahdars later failed and fell into arrears.
175.tq: Identify the legal-economic character of the holding created by a settlement arrangement.
xs: **Mootahdars** held the auctioned mootahs as **proprietary estates** after **1802** — option **(2)**.

xa: **Haveli** lands were under direct Company control (vs **Zamindari**).

175.s: Under which system were the Northern Circars mainly placed in the Madras Presidency?

xa: Haveli lands were grouped into **mootahs** and auctioned to **mootahdars**; many fell into arrears.

175.s: Which legislation provided for the full conversion of Zamindari estates into Ryotwari holdings in the Madras Presidency?

xs: Full conversion came with the **Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — option **(3)**.
**1793** made the zamindari settlement permanent — it created, not abolished, zamindaris.
xa: Some notes date zamindari abolition to **1952** (First Plan).

The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** dealt with **inam** (rent-free) titles.

175.s: In which year was the Permanent Settlement applied in the Circars and the Ryotwari system introduced in Rayalaseema?
175.x: These settlements came in 1802, after Guntur (1788), Padmanabham (1794) and the Ceded Districts (1800).
xa: The **Northern Circars** came earlier, in **1765-66**.
**Uyyalawada**'s revolt came in the **1840s**; zamindari abolition in **1948**.

175.x: The Northern Circars came in 1765–66 by Mughal farman and treaty with the Nizam; Guntur followed in 1788.

175.x: At Padmanabham in 1794 the Vizianagaram zamindar Vijayarama Gajapati Raju was defeated.

175.x: Moturpha was levied on professions, trades and looms of weavers, artisans and merchants.

175.x: Haveli was land under direct Company control; such lands were later brought under Ryotwari.

175.s: Why did rigid land revenue demands frequently push ryots towards moneylenders?
o: The government accepted revenue only in manufactured goods
Moneylenders alone were authorised to cultivate government land
Revenue had to be paid in cash even when crops failed
Ryots were prohibited from selling agricultural produce

xs: Revenue had to be **paid in cash even when crops failed** — option **(3)**.
This rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**, then mortgage and eviction.
xa: There was **no famine remission**, unlike the Mughal **zabt**.
Cash revenue forced **cash crops** (indigo, cotton, opium, jute).
Result: rural indebtedness and **land alienation**.

175.s: Which crops did the need to pay land revenue in cash encourage?
o: commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute
175.x: Cash revenue demands pushed peasants to grow commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, opium and jute.

175.s: Which pairing of newly strengthened rural classes with the areas in which they emerged is correct?
o: Merchant-landlords — Zamindari areas; moneylender-landlords — Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas
Moneylender-landlords — Zamindari areas; merchant-landlords — Ryotwari areas only
Artisan-landlords — all areas; merchants — no rural areas

175.x: Merchant-landlords became prominent in Zamindari areas, while moneylender-landlords emerged particularly in Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas.
175.tq: Match each rural class with the revenue system that enabled its rise.
xs: **Merchant-landlords** rose in **zamindari** areas; **moneylender-landlords** in **ryotwari and mahalwari** areas — option **(1)**.
Old zamindars lost estates to **urban merchants and moneylenders** at auction.
xa: The common result: **rural indebtedness + land alienation**.
Land became a **saleable commodity**, concentrated in few hands.

175.s: On what ground did Alice Thorner criticise the Ryotwari system?
o: abolished all direct contact between the state and zamindars
created a permanent landlord class in the Northern Circars
made the village community the sole unit of settlement
destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government
175.x: Alice Thorner argued that Ryotwari destroyed the village system and isolated individual farmers from the government.
175.tq: Associate a named critic with the precise argument attributed to her.
xs: **Alice Thorner** said ryotwari **destroyed the village system and isolated farmers from the government** — option **(4)**.
Making the village the unit is **Mahalwari**; a landlord class in the Circars is **zamindari**.
xa: Another criticism: the state became the **"ultimate landlord"**.

175.s: Absentee landlordism, sub-infeudation and rack-renting were the effects of which settlement?

175.s: Into what did the three major British land revenue settlements turn land?
175.x: The settlements made land transferable, created a loyal landlord class and fed rural indebtedness and peasant revolts.
xa: They shaped agrarian class structure that land reforms after **1947** tried to undo.
All three were **extractive**, with revenue in **cash** regardless of harvest.

175.x: The cotton slump after the American Civil War led to defaults and land passing to moneylenders.

175.s:
With reference to Ryotwari Settlement, consider the following statements
1. The rent was paid directly by the peasants to the government.
2. The government gave the Pattas to the Ryots.
3. The lands were surveyed and assessed before being taxed.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
175.x: All statements are correct: Under the Ryotwari Settlement (Munro System), the cultivator (ryot) was recognised as the owner of his land, subject to paying land revenue. The cultivators were registered and issued pattas. They were permitted to sell, lease, mortgage or transfer the right to land. Revenue settlement was directly made with the ryot. The land was surveyed carefully and separately before determining the revenue assessment. The settlement was periodically revised after 20 to 30 years, when the revenue demand was usually raised, taking into account changes in grain prices, marketing opportunities, irrigation facilities, etc. Ryotwari Settlement was introduced in parts of the Madras and Bombay Presidencies, Assam, and Burma.

176.x: The constant flow of wealth from India to England for which India did not get an adequate economic, commercial or material return has been described by national leaders and economists as ‘drain’ of wealth from India. Before 1813 company had a recurring surplus which accrued from (a) profits from oppressive land revenue policy (b) profits from its trade resulting from monopolistic control over Indian markets and exactions (c) made by the company’s officials. All this surplus was used by the Company as an “investment”, i.e. for making a purchase of exportable items in India and elsewhere. Against the exports of goods made out of this investment, India did not get anything in return. This system was brought to an end by the charter act of 1813. Barring a few exceptional years, a favourable balance of trade had been the normal feature of our foreign trade till the outbreak of world war II. 176.s: What was the chief economic foundation of the triangular commerce between India, China and England?
o: More than one of the above
176.x: The triangular trade between India, China, and England in the 18th and 19th centuries was centered on opium. The British East India Company established their monopoly in the cultivation of opium in the region of Bengal and Bihar etc., they forced the farmers to cultivate opium and exported it to China, where it was in high demand despite government bans. Profits from the opium trade were used to purchase Chinese goods like tea, silk, and porcelain for England, while manufactured goods from England were exported to India, completing the trade cycle. This exploitative system had severe social and economic consequences, including the Opium Wars between Britain and China. While commodities like silk and black pepper were also traded, opium was the chief economic foundation of this triangular commerce.

176.s: The artificially fixed rupee-sterling exchange rate prescribed by the Hilton-Young Commission (1926) was adopted by the British Government for which one of the following reasons?
o: Aiding the flow of remittances from India and maintaining India's creditworthiness
Encouraging the export of cotton produce from India
Preventing depreciation of the Rupee in terms of gold
176.x: Statement (a) is the correct answer: The Hilton-Young Commission recommended fixing the rupee-sterling exchange rate at 1s. 6d. (one rupee = 1 shilling and 6 pence). This was an artificially high (overvalued) rate compared to what many Indian nationalists and economists demanded (1s. 4d.). The British Government adopted this rate to facilitate the smooth and cheaper transfer of remittances from India to Britain. These included pensions of British officials, interest on public debt, military expenses, and dividends of British companies. A stronger rupee meant fewer rupees were needed to buy the required sterling for these remittances. It helped maintain India's creditworthiness in the London money market, making it easier for the Government of India to raise loans in Britain. Statement (b) is incorrect: An overvalued rupee made imported British goods cheaper for Indian buyers, benefiting British manufacturers and hurting Indian industries, which faced stiff competition from cheaper imports. Indian importers benefited, but this was not the main British motive. Statement (c) is incorrect: The artificially fixed high exchange rate hurt Indian exports (including cotton). Statement (d) is incorrect: The rate was fixed in relation to sterling, not primarily to prevent depreciation against gold. • Note: The Hilton-Young Commission (1926) has recently been in the news because 2026 marks the 100 th anniversary of its recommendations, which ultimately paved the way for the establishment

Which of the following led to the introduction of English Education in India?
1. Charter Act of 1813
2. General Committee of Public Instruction, 1823
3. Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
178.x: In 1823 A.D. the governor-general in council appointed a General Committee of Public Instructions, which had the responsibility to grant one lakh rupees for education. The committee consisted of 10 members, with Lord Macaulay as the President. Interestingly, during that time, there was a rapid change in attitude towards the composition of English education mainly due to the missionaries and the political influence of the English language. Thus, for the council of East India Company, the decision to grant money faced a greater problem. The controversy went on for 12 years. Even the General Committee of Public Instruction was also not able to decide the medium of instruction by vote, because out of 10 members, five were supporters of English language or Anglicists as the medium of instruction and the rest were supporters of the Classic language or Orientalists as a medium of instruction. This is the famous Anglicist and Orientalist controversy. As the President of the General Committee of Public Instruction, Lord Macaulay wrote a minute (detailed) where he made the conclusion regarding the controversy. By introducing the English language for the education of masses, Macaulay’s opinion was that the public mind of India might expand under the English system and through the English language it may educate the people into a capacity for better government.

178.s: Lord Macaulay was related to:
178.x: William Bentinck appointed a committee headed by Lord Macaulay to make recommendations for the promotion of education in India. In his report, Macaulay emphasized the promotion of European literature and science through English medium among the people of India. This recommendation was wholeheartedly accepted by William Bentinck. The Government Resolution of 1835 made English the official and literary language of India.

178.s: In the Hunter Commission report, special emphasis was laid on the development of:
178.x: Hunter Commission was founded under W.W. Hunter in 1882 A.D. to review the educational development after 1854 A.D. This Commission recommended the development of primary education. It was constituted by Lord Ripon. The Commission recommended for vocational training in secondary education and brought out the inadequate facilities available for female education in the country. The recommendations were partially implemented.

178.s: Sadler Commission was related to:
178.x: The Sadler Commission was related to education. In 1917, the British Government appointed a commission to study and report on the problems of Calcutta University. Dr. M.E. Sadler, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Leeds, was appointed its Chairman. The Commission included two Indian members, namely Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Zia-ud-din Ahmad. The Sadler Commission held the view that the improvement of secondary education was a necessary condition for the improvement of University education. It strongly criticized the University Act, 1904 and reported that there was no proper coordination between colleges and universities.

178.s: When was the ‘Sargeant Plan’ of education started ?
178.x: The Sargent Plan (Scheme) was presented in 1944 as a report on educational reforms. It was prepared to bring improvements in the field of education in India, and its main objective was to make the Indian education system more vocational and scientific in outlook. Its major recommendations included universal, compulsory, and free primary or basic education for all children between the ages of 6 and 14, divided into junior basic (6-11) and senior basic (11-14) stages.

to modernise the Indian people so that they could share their political responsibilities.

⚠ English Education Act **1835** = **Bentinck + Macaulay**; Wood's Despatch **1854** = **Charles Wood + Dalhousie**.

178.s: In whose reign was English Education introduced in India?
178.x: In 1823 A.D. the governor-general in council appointed a General Committee of Public Instructions, which had the responsibility to grant one lakh rupees for education. The committee consisted of 10 members, with Lord Macaulay as the President. Interestingly, during that time, there was a rapid change in attitude towards the composition of English education mainly due to the missionaries and the political influence of the English language. Thus, for the council of East India Company, the decision to grant money faced a greater problem. The controversy went on for 12 years. Even the General Committee of Public Instruction was also not able to decide the medium of instruction by vote, because out of 10 members, five were supporters of English language or Anglicists as the medium of instruction and the rest were supporters of the Classic language or Orientalists as a medium of instruction. This is the famous Anglicist and Orientalist controversy. As the President of the General Committee of Public Instruction, Lord Macaulay wrote a minute (detailed) where he made the conclusion regarding the controversy. By introducing the English language for the education of masses, Macaulay’s opinion was that the public mind of India might expand under the English system and through the English language it may educate the people into a capacity for better government.

178.s: The foundation of the modern educational system in India was laid by:
178.x: The foundation of the modern educational system in India was laid by Macaulay’s Minutes of 1835 A.D. (Issued on 2 February, 1835) In that minute, he commented on Sanskrit or Arabic by saying that “a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole literature of India and Arabia.”. Macaulay thus suggested making English the language of higher education in India with Western literature as the subject of study. Bentinck accepted his suggestion. Accordingly, on 7th March, 1835 A.D., a resolution passed by the Government declared: “His Lordship is of the opinion that the great object of the British Government ought to be the promotion of European literature and science amongst the natives of India and that all the funds appropriated for the purpose of education would be best employed on English education alone.” Bentinck’s Resolution opened a new chapter in the history of Indian education. 181.s:
Consider the following statements with reference to the ‘Revolt of 1857’ :
1. Syed Ahmad Khan wrote “Causes of the Indian Revolt”.
2. Mangal Pande was hanged on March 29, 1857.
3. Hazrat Mahal led the revolt at Lucknow.
4. Nana Saheb led the revolt at Bareilly.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
181.x: In 1857 AD, Kunwar Singh, associated with the contemporary zamindari of Jagdishpur in Bihar, led the rebellion. Thus, Statement 1 is correct. According to Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse, if an Indian ruler died without a biological heir, their kingdom would be annexed by the British East India Company. In 1853 AD, Jhansi's ruler, Raja Gangadhar Rao, died without a biological heir. Rani Lakshmibai adopted Damodar Rao as her son. However, the British refused to recognize the adopted son as the rightful heir and annexed Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1854 AD, making it a part of the British Empire.

182.x: Wajid Ali Shah was deposed when Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernance, costing lords, officials, retainers and soldiers their livelihoods.
xa: Awadh was the **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**, so its annexation angered high-caste sepoys.
About **21,000** taluqdars lost estates under the **Summary Settlement of 1856**.

182.s: Which of the following was an administrative cause of resentment before the Revolt of 1857?
o: Exclusion of Indians from high civil and military posts
Rapid and inexpensive justice for all social groups
Abolition of corruption in lower courts
Admission of Indians to all high civil and military posts
182.x: Indians were excluded from high civil and military posts, producing resentment against the colonial administrative structure.
xs: Indians were **excluded from high civil and military posts** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Justice was in fact **slow and costly**, and **corruption** was rampant in lower courts, so options 2 and 3 are wrong.
xa: Corruption was rampant in **lower courts and police**; justice **favoured the rich**.
Annexations threw thousands of **officials, retainers and soldiers** of princely courts out of work.
In the army an Indian could rise **no higher than Subedar**.

182.s: Rani Lakshmibai's grievance under the Doctrine of Lapse was that:
o: Her adopted son was refused the throne

182.s: What was a major consequence of the high and rigid land revenue demand on peasants?
o: They became independent of moneylenders and traders
They were driven into debt and lost land to moneylenders and traders
They were exempted from commercial cultivation
182.x: The heavy revenue burden pushed peasants into debt, often resulting in the loss of their land to moneylenders and traders.
182.tq: Follow the economic cause to its immediate social consequence.
xs: **Heavy, rigid land revenue** drove peasants into **debt**, and they **lost land to moneylenders and traders** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Revenue was collected rigidly under **Permanent/Zamindari**, **Ryotwari** and **Mahalwari** settlements.
xa: **Commercialisation** forced **cash crops** under high taxes.
Sepoys were **"peasants in uniform"** — they carried these rural grievances into the army.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** + **drain of wealth**.

182.s: Where was the Inam Commission of 1852, which confiscated about 20,000 estates whose owners could not show title, set up?
182.x: The Inam Commission (1852) worked in Bombay, not Madras, and confiscated some 20,000 estates lacking title.
xa: ⚠ **21,000** = taluqdars of Awadh (**1856**); **20,000** = Inam Commission estates (**1852**).
Result: a **fiercely anti-British landed class**.

182.s: What was the main reason for the ruin of Indian artisans and handicrafts before 1857?
o: The Industrial Revolution reduced the supply of British textiles
Indian handicrafts received increased princely patronage after annexations
British machine-made goods entered duty-free, while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs
British goods were excluded from Indian markets
182.x: After the Industrial Revolution, cheap British machine-made goods, especially textiles, entered India duty-free while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs, causing deindustrialisation. A and D reverse this, and B is wrong because annexations ended princely patronage.
182.tq: Compare unequal trade treatment rather than focusing on only one factor.
xs: **British machine-made goods entered duty-free**, while **Indian goods faced heavy tariffs** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This caused **deindustrialisation**; the Industrial Revolution **increased** cheap British goods, esp. **textiles**.
Annexations **ended** princely patronage, so option 2 is wrong.
xa: **Artisans were ruined** by cheap British goods.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** draining wealth to Britain.

182.s: What do the terms 'absentee sovereignty' and 'drain of wealth' refer to in the context of the causes of 1857?
o: the movement of peasants from villages to princely courts
the transfer of religious authority from temples to courts
the transfer of economic resources from India to Britain
the migration of British officials to Indian villages
182.x: Company rule was seen as 'absentee sovereignty', rule from distant Britain, under which India's wealth was drained to Britain. Both terms describe resources being transferred from India to Britain.
182.tq: Distinguish an economic concept from unrelated administrative or religious processes.
xs: Both terms describe **economic resources transferred from India to Britain** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** (rule from distant Britain) plus a **drain of wealth** to Britain.
xa: Peasants faced **heavy land revenue** and lost land to **moneylenders**.
Artisans were ruined by **duty-free** British goods.

182.x: About 21,000 taluqdars lost their estates in 1856; 20,000 is the number of estates taken by the Inam Commission.

182.x: The notes list the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act as 1856, so option (1) is correct. 1850 is the Lex Loci/Religious Disabilities Act, which is a different law.

182.x: The Religious (Caste) Disabilities Act was Act XXI of 1850; 1856 is the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act.

182.x: The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856 and challenged orthodox norms. Sati was abolished in 1829, the Caste Disabilities Removal (Lex Loci) Act dates to 1850 (1856 is a trap date for it), and the Charter Act grant was 1813.
xs: The **Hindu Widow Remarriage Act** was passed in **1856** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Sati** was abolished in **1829**; the **Caste Disabilities Removal Act** is of **1850** (**1856** is the trap date).

**1856** also = **General Service Enlistment Act** and the annexation of **Awadh**.

182.s: Which developments before 1857 generated fears of mass conversion among Indians?

Western education, railways and the telegraph
182.x: Western education, railways and the telegraph, along with missionaries preaching under police protection, created fears of mass conversion and loss of caste.

182.s: Which of the following was not a reason for making the sepoys of the East India Company rebellious?
o: The efforts of the officers of the company to spread
The order to the sepoys to travel on ships
182.x: The inefficiency of the officers was not a cause for the Sepoy Mutiny. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 occurred as a result of an accumulation of factors over time, rather than any single event such as an effort by officers to spread Christianity among the soldiers, which led to interference in the religious matters of the people. The order of the Company to the sepoys to travel on a ship was another reason as in Hinduism it was believed that travelling by sea could deprive them of their religious status of being a Hindu. A more immediate cause of the sepoy’s dissatisfaction was the recent order that they would not be given the foreign service allowance (Bhatta/Batta) when serving in Sindh or Punjab along with rumors of the use of animal fat in the cartridges of the New Enfield Rifle.

182.s: What was the approximate ratio of Indian sepoys to European soldiers in India on the eve of the Revolt of 1857?

182.s: When was the new Enfield Rifle with greased cartridges introduced in the British Indian Army?
182.x: The Company decided to use the new Enfield Rifle musket instead of old Brown Bess Standardised musket in December, 1856 A.D. The training for the use of this rifle was organized in Dum Dum, Ambala, and Sialkot. The rifle required an extraordinary kind of loading of a cartridge in the magazine and hence the soldiers while in the ensuing fight, had to bite off the outer covering of the cartridge while loading it down into the rifle’s muzzle. The cartridge was rumoured to have been greased with animal fat (Pig fat and Cow fat). The soldiers believed that this was an intentional act of the British to besmirch their religion. This became the immediate cause of the first Independence Struggle of India in 1857 A.D. 2. The immediate cause of India’s first war of independence was: (a) Doctrine of Lapse by Lord Dalhousie (b) Suspicion about British interference in religion (c) Military discontent (d) Economic exploitation of India R.A.S./R.T.S. 182.s: Which of the following has started the revolt of 1857?

182.s: The immediate cause of India’s First War of Independence was
o: Doctrine of Lapse by Lord Dalhousie.
Suspicion about British interference in religion.
182.x: The Enfield cartridges, rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat, made sepoys suspect British interference in their religion, and this triggered the revolt. The Doctrine of Lapse, military discontent and economic exploitation were long-term causes, not the immediate one.

182.s: The annexation of princely states became a cause of discontent before the Revolt of 1857 because it—
o: ended the drain of wealth to Britain
created employment for thousands of court officials and soldiers
restored the authority of all displaced rulers
threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work
182.x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
182.tq: Trace the administrative consequence of annexation.
xs: Annexations **threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They did the opposite of creating jobs; and Company rule kept the **drain of wealth** going.
xa: In Awadh (**1856**), the deposition of **Wajid Ali Shah** cost lords, officials, retainers and soldiers their livelihoods.
**Pindaris and irregular soldiers** were also disbanded.
Annexations also ended **princely/court patronage** of artisans.
