He attacked **Lt Baugh** and **Sergeant-Major Hewson** at **Barrackpore** on **29 March 1857**.
xa: He was hanged on **8 April 1857**; his regiment (**34th Bengal NI**) was disbanded.
On **21 July 2026** the PM paid tribute on his birth anniversary (born **19 July 1827**).
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** on **11-12 May 1857**.

Refusal to cross the sea to Burma

182.x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
182.tq: Distinguish the cause attached to a specific mutiny.

182.s: Why did the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle offend both Hindu and Muslim sepoys?
o: They were believed to contain cow and pig fat, and had to be bitten open.

182.x: The greased-paper cartridges were believed to contain cow fat, offensive to Hindus, and pig fat, offensive to Muslims. Sepoys had to bite them open before loading.
182.tq: Identify the religious implication of the practical loading procedure.
xs: The cartridges were believed to contain **cow and pig fat** and had to be **bitten** open — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cow** fat offended **Hindus**; **pig** fat offended **Muslims**.
xa: They were read as proof of a **colonial-missionary plot** to force conversion.
Rumours also spoke of **bone dust** in Company flour.

182.s: On which date did the Meerut rising of the Revolt of 1857 begin?

182.s: What immediately preceded the Meerut rising of 10 May 1857?

The disbandment of Mangal Pandey’s regiment
The refusal of the 19th Native Infantry to use the rifle
182.x: On 9 May 1857, 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut were sentenced to ten years. The rising followed on 10 May, when officers were shot and imprisoned comrades were freed.
182.tq: Identify the immediately preceding event rather than the later consequence.
xs: On **9 May 1857**, **85** sepoys of the **3rd Native Cavalry** were sentenced to **10 years** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The rising followed on **10 May**: officers shot, comrades freed, **"Delhi Chalo"**.
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed only after it (**11-12 May**); the other events were earlier.
xa: Mangal Pandey's regiment was disbanded on **8 April 1857**.
**19th NI** refused the cartridges at **Berhampur** in **February 1857**.

182.s: The rebels who reached Delhi on 11–12 May 1857 proclaimed whom as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan?
182.x: After reaching Delhi, the rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan on 11–12 May 1857.
182.tq: Match the political title with the associated leader.
xs: Rebels reaching Delhi (**11-12 May 1857**) proclaimed **Bahadur Shah II** **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kunwar Singh** was at Jagdishpur; **Wajid Ali Shah** had been deposed in **1856**; **Nana Sahib** was at Kanpur.
xa: They came from the **Meerut rising** (**10 May**) with the cry **"Delhi Chalo"**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar's successors were to lose the **Red Fort** and **royal title**.

182.s: When did the 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur refuse the new cartridges?
182.x: The Berhampur refusal came in February 1857; Vellore was July 1806, the Barrackpore mutiny November 1824 and Mangal Pandey's attack 29 March 1857.

Provisions of the Act are mentioned below – The company’s territories in India were to be governed by Queen, the company ceased to exercise its power and control over these territories. India was now to be governed in the name of the Queen. The Queen’s principal secretary of state for India received the powers and duties of the company’s court of directors. A council of fifteen members was appointed to assist the secretary of state for India. The Council became an advisory body for Indian affairs. For all communications between Britain and India, the secretary of the state became the real channel. The Crown was empowered to appoint a Governor-General and the Governors of the Presidencies. An Indian Civil Service was to be created under the control of the secretary of state. All the property and other assets of the East India Company were transferred to the crown. The crown also assumed the responsibilities of the company along with their related treaties, contracts and so forth.

The Battle of Padmanabham was fought on 10 July 1794 between the British East India Company and the Vizianagaram Zamindar, Maharaja Pusapati Vijayarama Gajapati Raju II. 187.s: Who were the palegars of the Ceded Districts?

Religious heads controlling the Wahabi Movement
Fortified military chiefs exercising autonomous power under the Nizam's nominal suzerainty

187.s: Which of the following was NOT among the principal causes of resistance by Palegars and other local groups?

187.s: Who was the principal officer responsible for suppressing the Palegar revolts in the Ceded Districts?

xs: **Thomas Munro**, **Principal Collector** (PYQ **2011**), suppressed the palegars — so option **(2)** is correct.

**Bentinck** was Madras Governor at **Vellore** (**1806**); **Cochrane** was **Kadapa Collector** in **1846**.

⚠ Some notes write "**Permanent Settlement**" here — an error; every other source gives Ryotwari.
xa: The Ryotwari was introduced by **Thomas Munro**.

187.s: What was the principal cause of the Vellore Mutiny?
o: The Company's takeover of Guntur from the Nizam
The introduction of Ryotwari settlement in the Ceded Districts

xa: Second cause: **Tipu's family** lodged in the fort.
Vellore = **first major sepoy revolt**, half a century before **1857**.

187.s: What was the immediate cause of Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt?
o: A ban on podu cultivation and toddy tapping
Takeover of his estate, reduction to a meagre pension, and the order to disarm and pay peshkash

Forcible conversion of local chiefs to Christianity

**Podu** and **toddy** restrictions belong to **Rampa 1879**; uniforms belong to **Vellore 1806**.

187.s: Who was the leader of the Wahabi movement, an anti-British movement by Andhra Muslims in the 19th century?
187.x:
Mubariz-ud-Daula, the brother of the Nizam of Hyderabad, became the chief supporter of the Wahabi Movement in Hyderabad State. Influenced by Syed Ahmed Barelvi, he attempted to organize resistance against growing British influence in the Deccan. His activities alarmed both the British and the Nizam's administration. Under British pressure, he was arrested and imprisoned, where he remained until his death. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Founder of Wahabi Movement → Syed Ahmed Barelvi
• Hyderabad leader → Mubariz-ud-Daula

187.s: The responsible person for the attack on Bollaram Residency during the Revolt of 1857 was
187.x: Turrebaz Khan, a local Hyderabadi leader, was responsible for leading the attack on the Bollaram Residency during the Revolt of 1857, targeting British forces stationed there. His actions reflected local resistance to British authority beyond the main theatres of the 1857 uprising. He is remembered as a freedom fighter from the erstwhile Hyderabad State.

xa: Their loyalty kept the revolt from spreading in the **Deccan**.
Rewards: **Star of India** for Afzal-ud-Daula; Salar Jung honoured.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
187.x:
Assertion (A) is false. It is incorrect to state that the Andhra region remained unaffected by the Revolt of 1857 because there were no local leaders. Although the revolt did not assume the same intensity as in North India, several local revolts and anti-British activities occurred in Andhra and the Hyderabad State. Leaders such as Turrebaz Khan in Hyderabad actively resisted the British, and anti-British sentiment was visible in different parts of the Telugu-speaking region. Therefore, the absence of local leaders was not the reason for the limited impact of the revolt.
Reason (R) is true. The Nizam of Hyderabad, Afzal-ud-Dowla (Asaf Jah V), remained loyal to the British during the Revolt of 1857. His cooperation helped the British suppress revolutionary activities in the Deccan and prevented the uprising from spreading widely in the Hyderabad State. The loyalty of the Nizam was one of the important reasons for the failure of the revolt in the Deccan. Since the Assertion is false and the Reason is true, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:

188.s: In which year Sati System was abolished by William Bentinck?
188.x: The meaning of Sati is ‘holy and virtuous woman.’ In Hindu rituals, the marriage is considered as Sanskar which means ‘relation of spirits.’ The Brahmins of the 18th century used to believe that if a woman became Sati, seven generations of his husband will achieve heaven. It was quite famous among highly reputed Brahmins, Kshatriya and Rajputs. Few conscious rulers of India also tried to abolish this system, Akbar was one of them. Marathas entirely abolished this system in the state. Portuguese and French also tried to abolish this system in Goa and Chandranagar respectively. It was Raja Ram Mohan Roy who started his campaign against Sati practice. The Bengal Sati Regulation, or Regulation XVII (17), A.D. 1829 of the Bengal Code was a legal act promulgated in Bengal Presidency. In 1830, this regulation was also implemented in Madras and Bombay Presidencies. Then Governor-General Lord William Bentinck which banned the practice of sati system.

190.x: The founder of Arya Samaj, Swami Dayanand Saraswati, used to believe in Vedic culture. He gave the slogan of 'Go back to Vedas' and attributed all the beliefs from the Vedic period until today as a false religion. 191.s: Who founded the ‘Theosophical Society’?
191.x: The Theosophical Society was founded in the year 1875 in New York City by Russian (Now-Ukrainian) noblewoman Helena Petrovna Blavatsky and American Colonel Henry Steel Alcott, along with William Quan Judge and some other individuals. In 1879, the principal founders, Madame H.P. Blavatsky and Col. Alcott moved to India where the Society spread rapidly. In 1882, they established the Society’s International Headquarter in Adyar, a suburb of Madras (currently Chennai). Brahmo Sabha was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828 and Ramkrishna Mission was founded by Swami Vivekananda in 1897, Thus, option (a) is correct.

In 1889 A.D., Annie Besant joined the society, and after coming to India in 1893 A.D., she played an active role in society. She considered Hinduism to be the world’s most esoteric and spiritual religion. She used to believe in the principles of rebirth.

191.x: first here. Rabindranath Tagore composed Jana Gana Mana in 1911. During his tour of South India in 1919, he stayed at the Theosophical College in Madanapalle, Andhra Pradesh, from 25 th February to 2 March, after being fatigued from Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 133 travel. While in Madanapalle, Tagore translated Jana Gana Mana into English as "Morning Song of India" on 28 th February 1919. It was here that Margaret Cousins, wife of James Cousins and then principal of the college, set the composition to music, transforming it from a lyric into a song. Tagore was deeply impressed by the institution and referred to the Madanapalle Theosophical College as the "Shantiniketan of South India." Eventually, Jana Gana Mana was officially adopted as India's national anthem on 24 th January 1950.

194.s: The Vital-Vidhvansak, the first monthly journal to have the untouchable people as its target audience was published by
194.x: Gopal Baba Walangkar was born in 1840 into a Mahar family near Mahad. An ex-army man, he was deeply influenced by Jyotirao Phule and adopted his ideas on social equality. Walangkar supported Phule's Aryan invasion theory and argued that the untouchables were the indigenous inhabitants of India, while the Brahmins were descendants of Aryans who had invaded the country. In 1886, Walangkar established the anti-caste organisation "Anarya Dosh-Parihar Samaj" to address the Dalit issues. In 1888, Walangkar started a monthly journal, Vital-Vidhvansak, which was the first to target the untouchables. He is credited with pioneering Dalit periodicals. Additional Information: In the 19 TH century, educated Indians started several journals. However, most of these were started by Brahmins and did not discuss the challenges faced by Dalits. This led to the emergence of Dalit periodicals, in which Dalits discussed their issues. Gopal Baba Walangkar, Shivram Janba Kamble, Kisan Fagu Bansode and Dr. Ambedkar played an important role in discussing Dalit issues in journals or periodicals. Founder/Editor Journal/Magazine Shivram Janba Kamble Somvanshiy Mitra (The friend of the depressed classes) Kisan Fagu Bansode Nirashrit Hind Nagarik, Vital Vidhwansak, Majur Patrika and Chokhamela Dr. B. R. Ambedkar Mooknayak, Bahishkrut Bharat, Samatha, Janata and Prabudhha Bharat

Gandhiji used to call Jamnalal his ‘fifth son.’ A loyal member of the Indian National Congress, Bajaj has worked extensively on social initiatives such as abolishing untouchability, the prohibition of Harijans into Hindu temples and promotion of Khadi. He participated in the Non-Cooperation Movement and renounced his title of ‘Rai Bahadur’ conferred by the British Government in 1921 A.D. In the same year, he succeeded in bringing Vinoba Bhave to Wardha to start a branch of Satyagraha Ashram. In 1923 A.D., in memory of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre, it was decided to organize tricolour flag procession in Nagpur and the Government banned it. Later, Jamnalal Bajaj took the challenge and organized the Flag Satyagraha and was sentenced to jail for 18 months and Rs. 3,000/- as fine. The leadership qualities he showed as the commander of Flag Satyagraha made him a real hero and a National leader.

195.s: Who was the founder of the first girls' schools at Rajahmundry?
195.x:
Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu was one of the greatest social reformers in Andhra Pradesh and is widely regarded as the Father of the Telugu Renaissance. At a time when female education was neglected, Veeresalingam took the pioneering step of establishing the first girls' school at Rajahmundry in 1874. He firmly believed that education was essential for the empowerment of women and for the progress of society. Apart from promoting women's education, he campaigned vigorously for widow remarriage, opposed child marriage, and fought against social superstitions. Through his writings, journals and reform movements, he laid the foundation for modern social reform in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

The comparison was made because both reformers worked tirelessly for widow remarriage, women's education, abolition of child marriage and social reform. Veeresalingam's efforts in Andhra closely resembled the reform movement led by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar in Bengal. This title recognizes Veeresalingam's pioneering contribution to modern social reform in Andhra Pradesh. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

195.s: Which of the following magazine was started by Veeresalingam?

The magazine focused primarily on women's education, widow remarriage, social reforms and the eradication of harmful customs. Through Janana and his other journals such as Vivekavardhini, Satihita Bodhini and Hasyasanjeevini, Veeresalingam spread progressive ideas and encouraged social awakening in Andhra. 195.s: Who formed the slave society in Andhra?

Brahma Naidu, the famous minister of the Palnadu Haihayas, introduced the institution known as Chapa Koodu, which promoted social equality by allowing people of different castes to dine together. He also organized a military force by recruiting people from different castes, including socially backward communities. Because of these reforms, he is often regarded as a pioneer of social equality in medieval Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).

195.s: Who founded the Varthamana Vyavaharikandhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samaj?
195.x:
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy founded the Varthamana Vyavaharika Andhra Bhasha Parivartaka Samaj to promote the use of spoken (Vyavaharika) Telugu instead of the highly Sanskritized classical language. He believed that education and literature should be written in a language easily understood by ordinary people. His movement revolutionized Telugu prose and greatly influenced modern Telugu literature, journalism and education. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

The school started in Mukherjee's home with 21 girls enrolled. The Bethune School was the second women's school in India (the first being in Bhidewada, Pune, by Jyotirao Phule). In December 1850, Bethune appointed Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar as the school's secretary. This appointment encouraged many Hindu families to send their girls to Bethune's school. The Bethune School was taken over by the government in 1856 and renamed in 1862-63 to honour its founder. In 1879, Bethune School was developed into Bethune College, India's first women's college. 198.x: In 1875, the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha submitted a petition to the British House of Commons demanding Indian representation in Parliament. It was founded in 1870 by Mahadev Govind Ranade, Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi, and S. H. Chiplunkar as a socio-political organisation in British India. Originally started in 1867 by Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi as a small body, it was later reorganised and renamed in 1870. The Sabha acted as a link between the colonial government and the Indian people by presenting public grievances and promoting patriotic feelings among the masses. It represented various sections of society, including sardars, landowners, businessmen, government servants, lawyers, and teachers. During the Deccan riots, the Sabha supported peasants and later organised famine relief in 1876. It also established nyaya sabhas (arbitration courts) for the private settlement of disputes, thereby reducing litigation costs. The organisation gradually expanded beyond Pune, opening branches in Satara district at Satara, Wai, and Karad.

199.s: Who was the founder of the Indian National Congress?
199.x: Allan Octavian Hume (A.O. Hume) was a retired British officer of Indian Civil Service. In 1884 A.D., he established the Indian National Union. After visiting Kolkata, Mumbai and Madras, Hume took the initiative to organize the first Indian National Union to meet in Poona. Its objective was to obtain a share in Government for educated Indians, to create a platform for civil and political dialogue between educated Indians in British Raj. The first meeting was scheduled to be held in Poona, but due to an outbreak of Cholera, it was shifted to Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay. The first session of Indian National Union was held on 28-30 December, 1885 A.D.. In this session on the advice of Dadabhai Naoroji, the organization was renamed as ‘Indian National Congress.’

199.s: The founder of the Indian National Congress was a :
199.x: Allan Octavian Hume (A.O. Hume) was a retired British officer of Indian Civil Service. In 1884 A.D., he established the Indian National Union. After visiting Kolkata, Mumbai and Madras, Hume took the initiative to organize the first Indian National Union to meet in Poona. Its objective was to obtain a share in Government for educated Indians, to create a platform for civil and political dialogue between educated Indians in British Raj. The first meeting was scheduled to be held in Poona, but due to an outbreak of Cholera, it was shifted to Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay. The first session of Indian National Union was held on 28-30 December, 1885 A.D.. In this session on the advice of Dadabhai Naoroji, the organization was renamed as ‘Indian National Congress.’

200.x: During the Moderate Phase (1885-1905 AD) of the Indian National Movement, there was support for the rich democratic and scientific culture of modern Europe. The moderate leaders advocated for constitutional reforms, political participation and the expansion of modern education. They supported English education, as they believed it would help develop a modern outlook and social progress in India. However, the growing masses viewed British colonial policies with increasing resentment. Notably, Dadabhai Naoroji strongly criticized the economic aspects of British colonialism. His book, "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India," highlighted issues related to the economic drain, heavy taxation, and the decline of Indian industries. The moderates attempted to address such concerns through constitutional means rather than direct confrontation.

202.s: Vande Mataram became the theme song of the Indian National Movement during –

The Kakinada Riot Case is regarded as the first criminal case registered in Andhra during the Vande Mataram Movement. The Vande Mataram Movement, inspired by the Swadeshi Movement following the Partition of Bengal (1905), spread nationalist ideas among students and the public. In Andhra, Kakinada emerged as one of the important centres of nationalist activity. The registration of the Kakinada Riot Case reflected the British Government's attempt to suppress the growing nationalist movement through legal action. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

203.s: The Tenali Bomb Case happened during which movement?
203.x:
The Tenali Bomb Case occurred during the Vande Mataram Movement, which gained momentum after the Partition of Bengal (1905). Incident Details
• A bomb explosion occurred on a footpath between the villages of Nandivelugu and Tenali.
• A local man named Chennugadu died on the spot from the blast.
• The trial court convicted a local resident named Chukkapalli Ramayya for the bombing and murder. It involved the application of early colonial explosives legislation, specifically the Explosive Substances Act of 1908 The movement encouraged boycott of foreign goods, promotion of Swadeshi and nationalist activities. Revolutionary incidents such as the Tenali Bomb Case reflected the growing militant phase of nationalism in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

204.s: Who among the following was the leader of the Moderates?
204.x: Gokhale The early Indian National Congress was divided into Moderates and Extremists. Gopal Krishna Gokhale was the leading figure of the Moderate faction. He believed in constitutional methods and gradual reform.

204.s: Who accused Indian National Congress of practising ‘politics of prayer, petition and protest’?
204.x: The first two decades are INC are described in history as a moderate era. Among some of the prominent moderate leaders were Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendra Nath Banerjee, Mahadev Govind Ranade, Pherozeshah Mehta, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Anand Mohan Bose. They had a sense of confidence in British justice and their generosity. Their aim was not aggressive nationalism for attaining independence. Leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, raised extremist ideology. B.G. Tilak accused moderates of believing in constitutional method and favouring the policy of protest, prayer, and petition.

204.s: Who among the following leaders was a supporter of ‘Swadeshi’?
204.x: Aurobindo Ghose was the main leader of Swadeshi Movement (started in 1905 A.D.) which began against the Bengal partition. Other main leaders of this movement were Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra) and Bipin Chandra Pal (Bengal).

204.s: The protest method of moderate leaders of the Congress was ?
204.x: The methods employed by the two groups (Moderates and Extremists) of Congress were different in their tempo and approach. Congress split into two different groups at Surat Session of Congress in 1907 A.D. While the moderates had infinite faith in the efficacy of constitutional agitation and in appealing to the British sense of justice and fair play, in holding an annual conference, making speeches, passing elaborate resolutions and sending deputations to England. The extremists had no faith in the benevolence of British public or Parliament, nor were they convinced of the efficacy of merely holding conferences. Extremists had faith in the concept of passive resistance.

204.s: Who among the following led the Swadeshi Movement in Delhi?
204.x: Syed Haidar Raja led the Swadeshi movement in Delhi; Tilak, Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh were not associated with Delhi in this role.

204.s: Who among the following was not known as a moderate in the National Movement?
204.x: Tilak was a militant Extremist leader, whereas Naoroji, Ranade and Gokhale were Moderates, so Tilak is the one not known as a moderate.

204.s: Which one of the following leaders belonged to the Extremist wing of the Congress?
204.x: Aurobindo Ghose was an extremist of Congress. He was one of the four pillars (Lal, Bal, Pal, Ghose) of extremists. He was arrested in 1908 A.D. by British Police in Maniktalla garden raid. He got the punishment of one-year imprisonment, but he was released due to the lack of evidence. Finally, he became sage, secluded himself from revolutionary activities and moved to Pondicherry (Puducherry).

204.s: The Congress policy of prayer and petition ultimately came to an end under the guidance of:
204.x: Congress policy of prayer and petition ultimately came to an end or reduced to minimum under the leadership of Bal Gangadhar Tilak. He was one of the strongest opponent of the British Empire. He strongly recommended a method of agitation. Many intellectual Congressmen became his followers. Leaders like Lala Lajpat Rai of Punjab and Bipin Chandra Pal of Calcutta turned into staunch followers of him. They strongly opposed the moderate policies of Congress.

204.s: The first leader to use the word ‘Swaraj’ was :

204.s: Who among the following was an extremist?
204.x: After the year 1906 A.D., the effect of extremism had increased on the Indian National Movement. The Congress split at Surat came in December 1907 A.D., around the time when revolutionary terrorism had gained momentum. The extremists were aggressive nationalist members of Indian National Congress. The important extremist leaders were Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghose. Tilak announced that ‘’ Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it’’.

The Extremists lacked faith in Moderate negotiations with the British. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #119 · pp 215-218]

Extremists were also called Assertive Nationalists. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #119 · pp 215-218]

**Constitutional agitation**, **negotiations** and **gradual self-government** belong to the **Moderates**.
The Extremists **lacked faith** in Moderate **negotiations** with the British.
xa: Extremists are also called **Assertive Nationalists**; their **influence increased** after **1906**.
Extremist **Swaraj** meant **complete freedom** from British control, not colonial self-government.

xa: ⚠ **3 Ps** (prayers, petitions, protests) = Moderates; **3 Ss** (self-reliance, self-sacrifice, strong will) = Extremists.

204.s: Four resolutions were passed at the famous Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in 1906. The question of either retention OR rejection of these four resolutions became the cause of a split in Congress at the next Congress session held at Surat in 1907. 204.x: The 1906 Calcutta Session of the Indian National Congress (INC) was a pivotal event in the Indian freedom struggle, marking the official shift from purely constitutional petitions to a more assertive nationalist agenda. Key Highlights:  President: The session was presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji, known as the "Grand Old Man of India". He was chosen as a compromise candidate to bridge the growing rift between the Moderate and Extremist factions of the Congress.  Adoption of 'Swaraj': For the first time, the word Swaraj (Self-government) was used from the Congress platform as the ultimate goal of the Indian people. Naoroji declared that Swaraj, along the lines of selfgoverning British colonies (such as Canada and Australia), was the "only and chief remedy" for India's problems. • The Four Resolutions: The session is most famous for passing four historic resolutions that defined the Swadeshi movement:  Swaraj: Demand for self-rule.  Swadeshi: Promotion of indigenous goods and industries.  Boycott: Refusal to use British goods as a political tool.  National Education: Establishment of an educational system under national control, free from colonial influence.

The Extremists, led by figures such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Aurobindo Ghosh, sought to expand the Swadeshi and boycott movements beyond Bengal and extend the boycott to all forms of association with the colonial government. On the other hand, Moderates, led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale and Dadabhai Naoroji, preferred to confine the movements to Bengal and limit the boycott to foreign goods. 204.x: Congress The Surat Split of 1907 was primarily the result of deep ideological differences between the Moderates and the Extremists within the Indian National Congress. 206.s: In which place Khudiram Bose tried to kill Kingsford?
206.x: Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki went to Muzaffarpur Bihar to assassinate Kingsford, Chief Calcutta Presidency Magistrate. Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki watched the usual movements of Kingsford and prepared a plan to kill him. On the evening of April 30, 1908 A.D., the duo waited in front of the gate of European club for the carriage of Kingsford to arrive. When a vehicle came out of the gate, they threw bombs and blew up the carriage. The revolutionary duo fled. Prafulla committed suicide and Khudiram was later arrested and hanged.

207.s: The Ghadr (Ghadar) was a
o: revolutionary association of Indians with headquarters at San Francisco.
militant organisation with headquarters at Berlin

207.x: In 1913, Indian revolutionaries living in the United States of America and Canada formed the Ghadar (Rebellion) Party. The majority of the party's members were Punjabi Sikh peasants and ex-soldiers who had come to North America in search of employment but experienced severe discrimination based on their race and economic status. The Association established a headquarters, Yugantar Ashram, in San Francisco and started a weekly paper, the Ghadar, for free circulation. • Aim: The Ghadar Party pledged to wage a revolutionary war against the British in India. • Ideology: Though most of the party's members were Punjabi Sikh peasants and ex-soldiers, the party's ideology was strongly secular. In the words of Sohan Singh Bhakna, who later became a major peasant leader of Punjab: "We were not Sikhs or Punjabis. Our religion was patriotism". • Presence: In addition to North America, particularly Canada and the United States of America, the party had active members in other countries such as Mexico, Japan, China, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Thailand, Indo-China, and East and South Africa. 208.x:
Annie Besant was a prominent Theosophist, educationist, social reformer and nationalist leader. She played a vital role in India's freedom movement through her writings, speeches and the Home Rule Movement. To spread nationalist ideas and mobilize public opinion, she founded two influential newspapers:
• New India – A daily newspaper that strongly advocated self-government, constitutional reforms and Indian nationalism.
• Common Weal – A weekly journal that discussed political, educational and social issues while supporting the Home Rule Movement. Through these newspapers, Annie Besant criticized British policies and inspired educated Indians to participate actively in the national movement. She also founded the Home Rule League in 1916 and became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress in 1917. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).

• Founder – Annie Besant
• Newspapers – New India and Common Weal
• Home Rule League – 1916
• INC President – 1917

During the Chirala–Perala Movement, Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya organized a disciplined volunteer corps known as the Ramadandu. The volunteers maintained law and order, organized public meetings, spread nationalist ideas and assisted people participating in the movement against British municipal taxation. The Ramadandu became a symbol of discipline, patriotism and non-violent resistance during the freedom struggle in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

210.s: Who was the leader of the Chirala– Perala Movement?
210.x:
The Chirala–Perala Movement (1921–22) was one of the earliest and most remarkable mass movements in Andhra during the Non- Cooperation Movement. The movement was led by Duggirala Gopala Krishnaiah, popularly known as "Andhra Ratna." The British Government decided to convert the twin towns of Chirala and Perala into a municipality and imposed heavy municipal taxes on the residents. Opposing the unjust taxation, Duggirala Gopala Krishnaiah inspired thousands of people to vacate their houses and settle outside the municipal limits rather than submit to British authority. To organize volunteers, he formed the famous Rama Dandu, which maintained discipline and coordinated the movement. Although the movement was eventually suppressed, it became a landmark in Andhra's freedom struggle and demonstrated the power of non-violent mass resistance. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Movement – Chirala–Perala (1921–22)
• Leader – Duggirala Gopala Krishnaiah
• Volunteer Force – Rama Dandu

210.s: Who led the Pedanandipadu Tax Refusal Movement?
210.x:
The Pedanandipadu Tax Refusal Movement was one of the important peasant movements during the Non-Cooperation Movement in Andhra. It was led by Parvataneni Veeraiah Chowdary, who organized peasants to refuse payment of land revenue to the British Government. Through disciplined volunteer groups, he mobilized villages and successfully resisted colonial authority. His fearless leadership earned him the popular title "Andhra Shivaji." The movement became a symbol of organized non-violent resistance in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:

• Movement – Pedanandipadu Tax Refusal Movement
• Title – Andhra Shivaji

210.s: "No Pullari (Grass) Tax" Movement was led in Palanadu by
210.x:
The No Pullari (Grass Tax) Movement was one of the important peasant agitations in the Andhra region during the freedom struggle. It was led by Kanneganti Hanumanthu in the Palanadu region of Guntur district. The British Government imposed a Pullari Tax, a tax collected from villagers for allowing their cattle to graze in forest lands. This tax severely affected poor farmers and cattle rearers whose livelihood depended on grazing rights. Kanneganti Hanumanthu organized the villagers and refused to pay the unjust tax. His courageous resistance made him a symbol of peasant protest against British oppression. During the agitation, British police opened fire, and Kanneganti Hanumanthu was martyred in 1922. His sacrifice inspired subsequent peasant movements in Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Movement – No Pullari (Grass Tax) Movement
• Leader – Kanneganti Hanumanthu
• Region – Palanadu
• Year – 1922

210.s: The first police station attacked by Alluri Sitarama Raju?
210.x:
The Rampa Rebellion (1922–1924), led by Alluri Sitarama Raju, began with a series of well-planned attacks on British police stations in the Agency areas of the Eastern Ghats. The first police station attacked was Chintapalli on 22 August 1922. The revolutionaries captured the police station and seized a large quantity of guns, rifles and ammunition, which were essential for continuing the armed struggle against the British. After Chintapalli, the rebels attacked the police stations at Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi, creating panic among the British administration. The Chintapalli attack is regarded as the formal beginning of the Rampa Rebellion. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• First Police Station Attacked – Chintapalli
• Date – 22 August 1922
• Movement – Rampa Rebellion

211.s:
Match Group – A with Group – B and select the correct answer using the codes given below.
Group – A (Book) Group – B (Author)

a. Japaneeyamu i. Gurajada Appa Rao

b. Mahaprasthanam ii. Sri Sri

c. Kanyasulkam iii. Puchalapalli Sundarayya

d. Veyipadagalu iv. Viswanatha Satyanarayana
v. Sriram Veerabrahmam
211.x:
Japaneeyamu was written by Sriram Veerabrahmam, reflecting his observations and thoughts on Japan and its society. Mahaprasthanam, the masterpiece of Sri Sri, revolutionized Telugu poetry by introducing progressive ideas and free verse. It remains one of the most influential works in modern Telugu literature. Kanyasulkam, authored by Gurajada Appa Rao, is regarded as the greatest social drama in Telugu literature. It exposed social evils such as child marriage, dowry and exploitation of women through satire and realistic characterization. Veyipadagalu, written by Viswanatha Satyanarayana, is one of the greatest Telugu novels. It portrays the gradual decline of traditional Indian society and is considered a classic of Telugu fiction. Thus, the correct matching is a–v, b–ii, c–i, d– iv, corresponding to Option (4).

215.s: After which movement was Tanguturi Prakasam called Andhra Kesari?
215.x:
During the Simon Commission protests held at Madras in 1928, Tanguturi Prakasam Pantulu displayed extraordinary courage by confronting armed British police. When the police threatened to fire on the protesters, Prakasam boldly opened his shirt and challenged them to shoot him. His fearless act inspired thousands of freedom fighters and earned him the title "Andhra Kesari" (Lion of Andhra). He later became the first Chief Minister of Andhra State after its formation in 1953. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Andhra Kesari – Tanguturi Prakasam
• Occasion – Simon Commission Protest (1928)

This act of defiance became iconic in the nationalist movement in Andhra. His courage during the protest cemented his image as a fearless leader.

216.s: What was the aim of Eka Movement in Oudh?

To protect the rights of landlords
216.x: The grassroot leadership of the Eka Movement was Madari Pasi and other low-caste leaders and many small Zamindars. Towards the end of 1921 A.D., peasant discontent resurfaced in some northern districts of the United Provinces—Hardoi, Bahraich, Sitapur etc. The issues involved were: (i) High rents—50 per cent higher than the recorded rates; (ii) Oppression by Thikedars in charge of revenue collection; and (iii) The practice of share-rents. The meetings of the Eka or the Unity Movement involved a symbolic religious ritual in which the assembled peasants vowed that they would: i. Pay only the recorded rent but would pay it on time; ii. Not leave when evicted; iii. Refuse to do forced labour; iv. No help to the criminals; v. Abide by Panchayat decisions. By March 1922 A.D., however, severe repression on the part of the authorities succeeded in bringing the Eka Movement to its end.

Through the Ryot Associations and later the Kisan Movement, he mobilized farmers across Andhra and brought their grievances into the national political arena. N. G. 219.s: Ulgulan Revolt was related to –
219.x: Munda Rebellion was one of the most prominent 19th-Century tribal rebellions in the subcontinent. Birsa Munda led this movement in the region in 1899-1900 A.D. The Ulgulan, meaning ‘Great Tumult,’ sought to establish an independent Munda Raj. The Mundas traditionally enjoyed a preferential rent rate as the Khuntkatti or the original clearer of the forest. But in the course of the 19th century, they had seen this Khuntkatti land system being eroded by the jaghirdars and thikedars coming as merchants and moneylenders. In 1895 A.D., Birsa claiming to have seen a vision of God, proclaimed himself a prophet with miraculous healing powers. Thousands flocked to hear the ‘new word’ of Birsa with its prophecy of an imminent deluge. The new prophet became a critic of the traditional tribal customs, religious beliefs, and practices. He called upon the Mundas to fight against superstition, give up animal sacrifice, stop taking intoxicants, wear the sacred thread and retain the tribal tradition of worship in the Sarna or the sacred grove. It was essentially a revivalist movement, which sought to purge Munda society of all foreign elements and restore its pristine character. Christianity influenced the movement as well and it used both Hindu-Christian idioms to create the Munda ideology and worldview. On Christmas Eve 1899 A.D., the Mundas shot arrows and tried to burn down churches over an area covering six police stations in the districts of Ranchi and Singhbhum. Next, in January 1900, t

219.x: One of the prominent revolts of the nineteenth century on the Indian subcontinent was the Munda Rebellion. This rebellion was led by Birsa Munda in Ranchi in the year 1899-1900. One was agrarian discontent and the other was the advent of Christianity. The movement aimed to reconstruct the tribal society from disintegration which was staring in its face due to the stress and strains of the colonial rule.

224.x: The real intention of the British to include the Princely States in the Federal Union proposed by the India Act of 1935 was to use the princes to counter balance the antiimperialist doctrines of the nationalist leaders. Princely States represented approx 25% of the population of India while under the Government of India Act, 1935 out of 260 members 156 were to represent the provinces and 104 to the Princely States in the Upper House and the Lower House consisted of 375 members out of whom 250 were to represent the provinces and 125 to represent the Princely States. In both Houses of the Federal Legislature, the states were given their quota of representation. But the members from the State were not to be elected. Despite such a wide range of provisions, the princely states however refused to join the Federation. They were alarmed by the changing situation in the country caused by the rapid spread of the National Movement. The British Government miserably failed to overcome the opposition of the Indian National Congress, the Muslim League and the princes against the Federal Scheme. So the Federal Scheme was withheld except the establishment of the Federal Court and the Provincial scheme was introduced on 1st April, 1937 causing a drastic change in the pattern of provincial politics.

224.x: Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 79 The Government of India Act 1919 introduced dyarchy at the provincial level, i.e. dual government in the provinces. Under this, the provincial administration was divided between reserved and transferred subjects. • Reserved List: The councillors nominated by the Governor controlled reserved subjects and were not responsible to the provincial legislature. It included key subjects such as defence (the military), foreign affairs, Police, justice, control over printing presses, irrigation, land revenue, factories, etc. • Transferred List: Transferred subjects were controlled by the ministers responsible to the provincial legislature. It included agriculture, health, Local self-government, education, and some departments relating to agriculture. • The residual powers were vested in the Governor-General in Council.

229.s: One common agreement between Gandhism and Marxism is:
o: The final goal of a stateless society
229.x: Both Gandhism and Marxism share the ultimate goal of achieving a stateless society, but their approaches and philosophies differ markedly. Gandhism envisions a stateless society founded on the principles of non-violence, truth, and simplicity. Gandhi advocated for establishing a self-governing society based on local, communitydriven institutions. Marxism, rooted in the ideas of Karl Marx, aims for a classless and stateless society as the final phase of human history. Marxists see the state as a tool of class oppression that should eventually dissolve after the working class (proletariat) takes control of the means of production. In Marxist thought, the stateless society is a communist one, characterised by common ownership of the means of production and the absence of social classes.

Traditionally, indigo was a natural dye extracted from certain plants, and India had been a major producer of indigo for the global market. Synthetic dyes offered cost-effective alternatives and could be produced in larger quantities, making them more attractive to manufacturers. As a result, the market for natural indigo became unprofitable, leading to a decline in its cultivation in India.

232.s: The first venture of Gandhi in all-India politics was the:

The scope of the area was also very limited. But Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919 A.D.) against the censure of freedom of press and detention without trial was proactively joined by all the sections of the society. Sentiments of the aggrieved common people were addressed. Knitting of people from all religions, all castes, all age groups, and both the genders in the Nationalist Movement had a distinguished characteristic of the Rowlatt Satyagraha. 233.s: The Hunter Committee was appointed after the:
233.x: The Government established a Disorders Inquiry Committee headed by Lord William Hunter, a Senator of College of Justice of Scotland. The Committee had 7 members 4 British and 3 Indians. It was set up to investigate the Jallianwala Bagh Tragedy. Before the Committee could publish its report, Congress put forward its view. This view criticized Dyer’s act as inhuman and also said that there was no justification for the introduction of the martial law in Punjab. 234.s:
Consider the following subjects with regard to Non- Cooperation Programme :
I. Boycott of law-courts and foreign cloth
II. Observance of strict non-violence
III. Retention of titles and honours without using them in public
IV. Establishment of Panchayats for settling disputes

234.x: The Non-Cooperation Programme was officially accepted by the Indian National Congress at the Calcutta Special Session in 1920 and then at the Nagpur Session in December 1920. The Non-Cooperation Programme accepted at the Nagpur Session included the following points – Renunciation of titles and honours; Boycott of law courts and foreign cloth; Establishment of panchayats to settle disputes; and the expectation that people strictly adhere to non-violence. The Congress and Gandhiji had called for a complete renunciation of the titles and honours given by the British government; there was no question of keeping them while merely avoiding their public use. Therefore, Statement III is incorrect. Hence, three out of the four statements are correct, and the correct option is (c).

237.s: Prabhavati Devi was the freedom fighter of which field?
237.x: The women of Bihar such as Prabhavati Devi, Rajvanshi Devi, Suniti Devi and Radhika Devi contributed to the Freedom Movement. Prabhavati Devi was a freedom fighter from Patna. Gandhi-Irwin Pact *Viceroy Irwin released Gandhiji from jail on 26th January 1931 AD considering the increasing influence of the Civil Disobedience Movement. Talks between Gandhiji and Irwin started in February 1931 AD with the efforts of Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jaykar. Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5th March, 1931. Sarojini Naidu termed Irwin and Gandhiji as ‘Two Mahatmas’. According to this pact - (1) Under the leadership of Gandhiji, Congress decided to withdraw the Civil Disobedience Movement, (2) All political prisoners who had not convicted of violence were to be released, (3) Right to peaceful protest at shops of foreign cloth and liquor shops, (4) Permission to make salt in the Coastal States without Salt Tax, (5) Congress agreed to participate in the Second Round Table Conference. People were disappointed by this pact because it did not include the commulation of the death sentences of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru. Biographer of Irwin, Alan Campbell Johnson termed the benefits to Gandhi in Gandhi-Irwin Pact as consolation prizes and said this pact was the only surrender of Irwin agreeing to enter into negotiations. 1. In which year did the famous Gandhi-Irwin Pact take place? (a) 1929 A.D. (b) 1930 A.D. (c) 1931 A.D. (d) 1932 A.D. (e) None of the above/More than one of the above 67th

238.s: Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam were known for their production of
238.x:
Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam, located in the present-day Prakasam district, were historically famous for salt production. Their coastal location and extensive salt pans made them important centres for manufacturing and trading salt during both the pre-colonial and British periods. Salt production formed an important part of the local economy, and the region contributed significantly to the salt trade along the Coromandel Coast. During the British period, salt became an important source of government revenue through the imposition of the Salt Tax, which later became the focus of Gandhiji's Civil Disobedience Movement. Although the region also engaged in agriculture and trade, Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam are particularly remembered for their salt industry. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

• Chinaganjam – Salt production
• Present District – Prakasam

241.x: The failure of the Cripps Mission made it clear that Britain was not ready to give India any real Constitutional advance. In May 1942, Gandhiji drafted a resolution calling for British withdrawal and non-violent noncooperation in the face of any Japanese invasion. In July, the Congress Working Committee (CWC) at Wardha adopted the Resolution (later known as the Quit India Resolution), which was to be ratified at the Bombay All India Congress Committee (AICC) meeting in August. On 8 th August 1942, the AICC at Gowalia Tank in Bombay, passed a historic Quit India resolution. The resolution demanded an immediate end to British rule in India. Subsequently, on 9 th August 1942, the British Government, invoking the Defence of India Rules, arrested Gandhi along with members of the Congress Working Committee and other leaders. The Working Committee, the All- India Congress Committee, and the four Provincial Congress Committees were deemed illegal associations under the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1908.

243.s: In which year was the Indian National Army founded?
243.x: In February, 1942 The Indian National Army was formed under the leadership of Mohan Singh. He was the first commander of Azad Hind Fauz. The unit was dissolved in December, 1942 after apprehensions of Japanese motives with regard to the INA led to disagreements and distrust between Mohan Singh and INA leadership on the one hand and the League’s leadership, most notably Rash Behari Bose on the other. A large number of the INA’s initial volunteers however, later went on to join the INA in its second incarnation under Subhash Chandra Bose. Bose arrived in Singapore on 2 July 1943 and on 4th July, 1943, Rash Behari Bose gave the command of I.N.A. to Subhash Chandra Bose. In October, 1943 Bose formally announced the establishment of the Provisional Government of Free India and took charge of INA.

Campaign for the Release: In its Bombay session in September 1945, the All India Congress Committee (AICC) declared its support for the INA soldiers. The Congress established the INA Defence Committee to defend the INA prisoners. It included famous lawyers such as Bhulabhai Desai, M. Asaf Ali, Tej Bahadur Sapru, K.N. Katju, and Jawaharlal Nehru. In addition to legal help, Congress organised relief funds and arranged employment for the INA men. There was a countrywide protest against the trial of three INA heroes (Sehgal, Shah Nawaz and Dhillon) belonging to the Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 126 Hindu, Muslim and Sikh communities, symbolising the unity of the people. The Commander-in-Chief, Claude Auchinleck, was forced to remit the sentences due to prevailing circumstances. Later, all three defendants were released. This case became a symbol of the country's freedom struggle and showed the strength of Unity.

After the end of the war, Colonel Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, Colonel Prem Kumar Sahgal and General Shahnawaz Khan were put on trial in Delhi for waging war against the British Empire. Rashid Ali was sentenced to seven-years imprisonment while other prisoners faced the transportation for life punishment. The defence of the INA prisoners was taken up by the Congress and Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, K.N. Katju, Jawahar Lal Nehru and Asaf Ali appeared in court at the historic Red Fort trials. The growing Nationalist sentiments developed into violent confrontations with authority and pressure from the political parties from India; Commanderin-Chief Field Marshal Sir Claude Auchinleck was forced to let the defendants go free.

249.x: The Radcliffe Line was the boundary between the Indian and Pakistani portions of the Punjab Province and Bengal Presidency of British India. 252.s: What was Ambedkar's critique of caste in Annihilation of Caste?
o: Only untouchability needed to be removed while the caste system could remain.
Caste had no connection with religious texts and could be reformed through charity alone.
The caste system as a whole had to be destroyed because it possessed religious sanction in the Shastras and Vedas.
Caste was an ideal division of labour that required only greater efficiency.
252.x: Ambedkar argued that caste had religious sanction in the Shastras and Vedas and that reform limited to untouchability was inadequate; the entire caste system had to go.
252.tq: Choose the option that captures both the source of caste sanction and the scope of the remedy.
xs: In **Annihilation of Caste**, the **caste system as a whole had to be destroyed** because it had **religious sanction in the Shastras and Vedas** — option **(3)** is correct.
Since the sanction was religious, Ambedkar held **reform within Hinduism futile**.
Removing only **untouchability** was not enough — the **whole caste system** must go, so option (1) is wrong.
Varna as an ideal **division of labour** was **Gandhi's** view, not Ambedkar's.
xa: The book was a **direct rebuke of Gandhi's approach**.
⚠ Gandhi: varna a **division of labour**; Ambedkar: caste a **division of labourers**.
"Nothing can emancipate the outcaste except the **destruction of the caste system**" — Ambedkar (**APPSC-G1 2018**).
Remedy prescribed: **inter-caste marriage**.

252.s: On which of the following did Gandhi and Ambedkar differ fundamentally?
o: Whether the whole caste system should be annihilated
252.x: Both sought uplift of the marginalised and stressed education, but differed on whether the whole caste system should be annihilated.
xa: Gandhi called **untouchability a corruption** of varna.
Ambedkar's education slogan: "**Educate, Agitate, Organise**".
Ambedkar founded the **People's Education Society (1945)**.

252.s: Who described caste as “not just a division of labour, but a division of labourers”?
252.x: The statement that caste is a division of labourers, rather than merely a division of labour, was made by B.R. Ambedkar.
252.tq: Use author-quotation matching, a common history question pattern.
xs: **B.R. Ambedkar** described caste as "not just a **division of labour**, but a **division of labourers**" — option **(3)** is correct.
**Gandhi** held the opposite: **varna** was an ideal **division of labour** and only untouchability a corruption.
**B.S. Moonje** and **Malaviya** appear in the notes only in the debate on Ambedkar's turn to **Sikhism** (Moonje for, Malaviya against).
xa: ⚠ Classic trap: Gandhi = division of **labour**; Ambedkar = division of **labourers**.
Ambedkar: "Nothing can emancipate the outcaste except the **destruction of the caste system**" (**APPSC-G1 2018**).
His remedy: **inter-caste marriage**, the "**real remedy**".

252.s: On which date did Ambedkar call the Indian village 'a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism' in the Constituent Assembly?
252.x: He said this on 4 November 1948, preferring the individual, not the village, as the basic unit.
xa: He **rejected Gram Swaraj** and trusteeship, favouring a **strong, centralised constitutional democracy**.
Gandhi stood for decentralised **Gram Swaraj**; Ambedkar for a **strong Centre**.
The strong Centre was meant to **protect minorities**.

252.s: What was Ambedkar's position regarding political power for the Depressed Classes?
o: Political power was necessary to protect their interests.
Political power could be secured only through religious conversion.
Political power should remain exclusively with caste Hindus.
Political power was irrelevant because social reform alone was sufficient.
252.x: Ambedkar held that political power was necessary for the Depressed Classes to protect themselves and secure their rights.
252.tq: Test the central argument associated with a political thinker.
xs: Ambedkar held that **political power was necessary** for the depressed classes **to protect themselves** — option **(1)** is correct (**APPSC GS 2016**).
This is why he **demanded separate electorates**, against Gandhi.
He did not see social reform alone as enough: his method was **legal, constitutional, political rights** and state action.
xa: **Poona Pact (1932)**: he settled for joint electorates with **147** reserved seats.
Later he felt the Pact made Dalits **dependent on caste Hindus**.
He founded the **Independent Labour Party (1936)**.

252.s: According to Ambedkar's Who Were the Shudras?, who were the Shudras originally?
o: A Kshatriya community degraded after conflict with Brahmins
An occupational group created by British legislation
A group formed exclusively from foreign invaders
252.x: Ambedkar argued that the Shudras were originally Kshatriyas who were degraded after conflict with Brahmins, who denied them the upanayana.

**What Congress and Gandhi Have Done** (**1945**) attacked Congress; **The Buddha and His Dhamma** (**1957**) reread Buddhism.
xa: ⚠ Shudras = degraded **Kshatriyas**; Untouchables = "**broken men**".
**Thoughts on Linguistic States** — **1955**.
**Annihilation of Caste** — **1936**.

252.s: Why did Ambedkar propose that State socialism should be written into the Constitution?
o: To ensure that a legislative majority could not undo it
To place economic policy exclusively under local bodies
To permit every village to frame a separate economic constitution
To prevent all state ownership of industries

xs: So that **a legislative majority could not undo it** — option **(1)** is correct.
The proposal is in **States and Minorities (1947)**.
It called for **state ownership of key industries**, so option (4) is the reverse of his plan.
xa: Also: state ownership of **agricultural land**, let out for **collective farming**.
**Nationalised insurance**.
He favoured a **strong Centre**, not local bodies, so option (2) is wrong.

252.x: Ambedkar rejected Gram Swaraj and trusteeship, favouring a strong, centralised constitutional democracy to protect minorities.

252.s: Who advocated ‘Neo-Buddhism’?
252.x: Navayana/Neo-Buddhism means "new Vehicle" and refers to the re-interpretation of Buddhism by B.R. Ambedkar. Navayana rejects practices and precepts such as renouncing monk and monasticism, Karma, rebirth after life, samsara, meditation, enlightenment and four noble truths considered to be foundational in the Buddhist traditions. It revises the original Buddha's teachings about class struggle and social equality.

**CGPSC 2019** asked it as Neo-Buddhism = Ambedkar.
Its basis is **The Buddha and His Dhamma** (posthumous, **1957**), a rational, social reading of Buddhism.
xa: It gave rise to the **Dalit Buddhist Movement**.
Conversion: **14 October 1956**, **Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur**, with **22 vows**.

255.s: On whose plea did Swami Sitaram end his hunger strike?

Swami Sitaram actively campaigned for the formation of a separate Andhra State and undertook a hunger strike to press this demand. He eventually withdrew his fast at the request of Acharya Vinoba Bhave, who appealed to him to end the agitation through peaceful and constitutional means. Vinoba Bhave's intervention played a significant role in persuading Swami Sitaram to discontinue his fast. Although the demand for Andhra State continued, it was later Potti Sreeramulu's fast unto death that ultimately led to the formation of Andhra State on 1 October 1953. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

255.s: When did Potti Sriramulu become Amarajeevi?

Amarajeevi Potti Sriramulu sacrificed his life on 15 December 1952 after undertaking a 58- day fast unto death demanding the formation of a separate Andhra State. His martyrdom triggered widespread protests across the Telugu-speaking regions, compelling the Government of India to announce the formation of Andhra State, which came into existence on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as its capital. Potti Sriramulu is remembered as "Amarajeevi" for his supreme sacrifice. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

255.s: Andhra State was formed on
255.x:
Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953 by separating the Telugu-speaking districts from the erstwhile Madras State. It became the first linguistic state to be created in independent India. The formation of Andhra State was the culmination of a long struggle for a separate Telugu-speaking province. The movement reached its peak after the fast unto death by Potti Sreeramulu, who sacrificed his life on 15 December 1952 demanding a separate Andhra State. His martyrdom led to widespread protests, compelling the Government of India to accept the demand. Kurnool became the capital of the newly formed Andhra State, while the High Court was established at Guntur. Later, on 1 November 1956, Andhra State was merged with the Telugu-speaking districts of Hyderabad State to form Andhra Pradesh under the States Reorganisation Act. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Andhra State – 1 October 1953
• First Linguistic State in Independent India
• Capital – Kurnool
• High Court – Guntur

255.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:

A. Formation of the Visalandra Mahasabha

B. Dhar Commission

C. Swami Sitaram's fast

D. Formation of States Re-organization Commission
255.x:
The demand for a separate Andhra State and later a Visalandhra gained momentum after Independence through a series of political developments. The Dhar Commission was appointed in 1948 to examine the question of linguistic provinces. It did not recommend the formation of states on a linguistic basis. In 1949, the Visalandra Mahasabha was formed to campaign for the unification of all Telugu-speaking areas into a single state. Swami Sitaram undertook his fast in 1951 demanding the formation of Andhra State, which further intensified the movement. The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) was constituted in 1953 under the chairmanship of Justice Fazl Ali to examine the reorganisation of states on linguistic and administrative grounds. Its recommendations eventually led to the formation of Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956. Thus, the correct chronological order is: Dhar Commission → Visalandra Mahasabha → Swami Sitaram's Fast → States Reorganisation Commission Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Dhar Commission – 1948
• Visalandra Mahasabha – 1949
• Swami Sitaram's Fast – 1951
• States Reorganisation Commission – 1953

The Srikrishnadevaraya Andhra Bhasha Nilayam, established in Hyderabad in 1901, was one of the earliest Telugu libraries in the Hyderabad State. It played a crucial role in promoting Telugu language and literature. The Vignana Chandrika Grandhamandali was founded in Hyderabad in 1906 to publish books and encourage intellectual activity among Telugu-speaking people. The Andhra Council of Research was established at Kovvur in 1916 with the objective of encouraging historical and literary research relating to Andhra. The Andhra Saraswati Parishad, founded in Hyderabad in 1922, became an important institution for promoting Telugu language, literature and education. Thus, the correct matching is a–II, b–III, c–I, d– IV, corresponding to Option (3).
Exam Note: Prominent libraries and literary bodies established across Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema:
• Saraswathi Mahal Library (Thanjavur, 1700s): While located in Tamil Nadu, it holds one of the most vital historical collections of ancient Telugu palm-leaf manuscripts preserved by the Raghunatha Nayaka kings.
• Gautami Regional Library / Gautami Grandhalayam (Rajahmundry, 1898): Formed by merging the Vasuraya Grandhalayam and the Town Hall Library. It is one of the oldest public libraries in the state.
• The Reading Club (Kolluru, Guntur, 1899): One of the earliest rural library initiatives in the Guntur district.
• Youngmen's Literary Association (Guntur, 1900): Created to foster intellectual dialogue and provide access to newspaper

The Gentlemen's Agreement was signed on 20 February 1956 by representatives of Andhra State and Telangana before the formation of Andhra Pradesh. Signatories included leaders such as Alluri Satyanarayana Raju, Bezawada Gopala Reddy, Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, Marri Chenna Reddy and J. V. Narsinga Rao. 262.s: According to the Gentlemen's Agreement, what was the ratio of Cabinet representation for Andhra and Telangana?
262.x:
The Gentlemen's Agreement, signed in 1956 before the formation of Andhra Pradesh, was intended to safeguard the interests of the Telangana region after its merger with Andhra State. One of its important provisions related to the composition of the State Cabinet. It provided that the Cabinet should consist of ministers in the ratio of 60:40 between Andhra and Telangana, reflecting the relative population of the two regions while ensuring adequate representation for Telangana. The Agreement also included safeguards relating to public employment, expenditure, education and the establishment of the Telangana Regional Committee. Therefore, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note: Important provisions of the Gentlemen's Agreement:
• Cabinet Ratio – 60 : 40
• Telangana Regional Committee
• Safeguards in employment and education
• Protection of Telangana's financial interests

262.s: Who was the Chief Minister during the Separate Telangana Movement in 1969?
262.x:
The Separate Telangana Movement of 1969 took place during the tenure of Kasu Brahmananda Reddy, who served as the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh from 1964 to 1971. The movement arose due to dissatisfaction over the implementation of safeguards promised under the Gentlemen's Agreement and issues relating to employment, education and regional development. The movement became one of the most significant regional agitations in the history of Andhra Pradesh. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

262.s: Which of the following is incorrect about Damodaram Sanjivayya?
o: He was never defeated in an election.
He was the second Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh.
He served as the President of the Indian National Congress.
Worked as a minister in Andhra Pradesh Government.
262.x:
Damodaram Sanjivayya was the second Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh (1960– 1962) and the first Dalit Chief Minister of any Indian State. He later became the President of the Indian National Congress (1962–1964) and also served as a Union Minister. The statement that he was never defeated in an election is incorrect, as he did suffer electoral defeats during his political career. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

• Second Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh
• First Dalit Chief Minister in India
• INC President (1962–64)

262.s: Who was the first Dalit Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh?
262.x:
Damodaram Sanjivayya became the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh in 1960, making him the first Dalit Chief Minister not only of Andhra Pradesh but also of any Indian State. His achievements include:
• Served as Chief Minister (1960–1962)
• Became President of the Indian National Congress (1962–64)
• Later served as Union Labour Minister
• Worked extensively for labour welfare and social justice. His rise from a humble background to the highest political offices remains a landmark in Indian politics. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• First Dalit CM of India – Damodaram Sanjivayya
• INC President – 1962–64

262.s: During whose reign did N. T. Rama Rao establish the Telugu Desam Party?
262.x:
The Telugu Desam Party (TDP) was founded by Nandamuri Taraka Rama Rao (N. T. Rama Rao) on 29 March 1982 with the objective of protecting Telugu self-respect (Telugu Atma Gauravam) and providing an alternative to the Congress Party. At the time of the party's formation, Bhavanam Venkatarami Reddy was the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh. He served as Chief Minister from 24 February 1982 to 20 September 1982. Within a short period of its formation, the Telugu Desam Party achieved a historic victory in the 1983 Andhra Pradesh Assembly Elections, bringing N. T. Rama Rao to power. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:

The Gentlemen's Agreement was signed on 20 February 1956 between the leaders of Andhra State and Telangana. The agreement provided safeguards for Telangana regarding employment, education, expenditure and political representation before the formation of Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956. Exam Note:
• Gentlemen's Agreement – 20 February 1956 The 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement was signed by 8 key political leaders representing the Andhra and Telangana regions on February 20, 1956, to safeguard Telangana's interests prior to the formation of unified Andhra Pradesh. Signatories from Andhra Region
• Bezwada Gopal Reddy – Chief Minister of Andhra State
• Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy – Andhra Congress leader (later Chief Minister and President of India)
• Gouthu Latchanna – Andhra leader and minister
• Alluri Satyanarayana Raju – Andhra Congress committee leader Signatories from Telangana (Hyderabad State) Region
• Burgula Ramakrishna Rao – Chief Minister of Hyderabad State
• K. V. Ranga Reddy – Telangana political leader
• Marri Channa Reddy – Telangana leader (later Chief Minister of undivided AP)
• J. V. Narasing Rao The key provisions ensured financial protection, job security, and regional autonomy for Telangana. Finances and Development
• Surplus Revenue: Extra money earned from the Telangana region must be spent only on the development of Telangana.
• Shared Expenses: State administration costs were to be split proportionally between the two regi

263.s: President Rule was imposed in Andhra Pradesh in 1973 because of:
263.x: Jai Andhra Movement President's Rule was imposed in Andhra Pradesh in 1973 following the Jai Andhra Movement, a separatist agitation in the Andhra region demanding a separate state. This followed widespread unrest and breakdown of normal administration. It was one of several instances of political turbulence in the state's history.

263.s: How did the Jai Andhra Movement end in 1972–73?
o: With the abolition of Mulki Rules
With the arrests of many student and women leaders
As the Central forces suppressed the movement
With the Six-Point Formula proposed by the Central Government
263.x:
The Jai Andhra Movement (1972–73) emerged in the Andhra region in response to the implementation of the Mulki Rules, which gave preference to local candidates in public employment in Telangana. The movement demanded either the abolition of the Mulki Rules or the creation of a separate Andhra State. It witnessed widespread protests, demonstrations and political instability. To resolve the regional tensions, the Central Government introduced the Six-Point Formula in 1973. The formula aimed to ensure balanced regional development, provide equitable opportunities in education and employment, and reduce regional disparities. It eventually replaced the earlier safeguards and brought the movement to an end. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Jai Andhra Movement – 1972–73
• Ended with – Six-Point Formula (1973)
• Objective – Regional balance and employment safeguards

Many people in the Andhra region viewed the judgment as discriminatory, leading to widespread protests demanding either the abolition of the Mulki Rules or the creation of a separate Andhra State. The movement ultimately led to the Six-Point Formula (1973) as a political solution. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).

268.x:
Viswanatha Satyanarayana became the first Telugu writer to receive the Jnanpith Award, India's highest literary honour, for his monumental work Ramayana Kalpavriksham. The work is regarded as one of the greatest literary reinterpretations of the Ramayana in Telugu and reflects Viswanatha's profound scholarship, classical style and philosophical depth. Besides this masterpiece, he authored numerous novels, poems, dramas and literary essays, making him one of the most prolific writers in Telugu literature. Later, Dr. C. Narayana Reddy also received the Jnanpith Award for his poetic work Viswambhara, but he was not the first Telugu recipient. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).

**Gussadi** = **Gond** (Telangana side).

272.s: In Chenchu society, who officiate marriages along with the Raju and the Mantri?
272.x: Raju, Mantri and Kolagadu, from different clans, officiate marriages; Bhoomani and Kumakula are clans.

272.s: Idital wall paintings are associated with which tribal community?
272.x: Idital wall paintings are associated with the Savara, also known as Sora, community.
272.tq: Match a distinctive art form with its tribal community.
xs: **Idital** wall paintings belong to the **Savara (Sora)** — option **(3)**.
**Gond** art is from **MP**; **Pithora** is of the **Rathwa** (Gujarat-MP).
xa: Other tribal arts: **Warli** (Maharashtra), **Bhil**.

Agency crafts include **bamboo work**.

272.s: With which tribe is Pithora painting particularly associated?
o: Rathwa of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh
272.x: Pithora is associated with the Rathwa community of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.
272.tq: Identify the community and region linked with a named art tradition.
xs: **Pithora** is the art of the **Rathwa** (**Gujarat-MP**) — option **(2)**.
**Warli** is Maharashtra's art; the **Savara** paint **Idital**; the **Koya** are known for the **Kommu** dance.
xa: **Gond** art is from **MP**.
**Bhil** art is another comparison form.
**MP** has the largest tribal population.

272.s: On which of the following does the agency economy of the Araku belt rest?
o: Podu, minor forest produce, coffee and horticulture
Tea plantations, jute mills and inland shipping
Marine fishing, salt production and shipbuilding
272.x: The agency economy combines podu (shifting cultivation) and minor forest produce with coffee and horticulture in the Araku belt.
xa: Agency crafts: **bamboo work**.
**Idital** wall paintings of the **Savara (Sora)**.
Araku tribes' spring festival: **Eetela Panduga (Chaitrapurab)**.

272.s: In the agency areas, what does 'Podu' refer to?
272.x: Podu is the shifting cultivation of the agency areas.

272.s: Which tribal community of Andhra Pradesh is traditionally known for basket making?
272.x: The Yerukala are traditional basket makers, weaving baskets from bamboo and wild date palm spines.

272.s: With which of the following is Eetela Panduga, also known as Chaitrapurab, associated?
o: the harvest festival of the Lambadas
the birth ceremony of Koya boys
the spring festival of the Araku tribes
272.x: Eetela Panduga or Chaitrapurab is the spring festival of the Araku tribes, during which Dhimsa is danced.
272.tq: Link a regional festival with its tribe and season.
xs: **Eetela Panduga (Chaitrapurab)** is the **spring festival of the Araku tribes** — option **(3)**.
**Dhimsa** is danced at it (**Aug 2026**).
Newborn-son rites are **Heli Panduga** (Lambadi); **Modakondamma** is a separate **Paderu** jatara.

Lambadi Deepavali = **Kalimas**.
Dhimsa region: **ASR** and **Parvathipuram Manyam**.

272.s: What do the Lambadis call Deepavali?
272.x: The Lambadis call Deepavali Kalimas; Jari Gundu is another name for Heli Panduga.
xa: Seethala Panduga falls in **Ashada**; **Seethala Mata** guards against **smallpox**.
**Lambadi** dance: Lambada/Sugali (Banjara) **women**.
Araku tribes' spring festival: **Eetela Panduga**.

272.s: Modakondamma, in whose honour an annual tribal jatara is held, is the goddess of which region?
272.x: Modakondamma is regarded as the goddess of the Paderu agency, where an annual tribal jatara is held.
xa: Araku tribes celebrate **Eetela Panduga (Chaitrapurab)** in spring.
**Dhimsa** belongs to **ASR** and **Parvathipuram Manyam**.
Lambadi festivals: **Seethala Panduga**, **Heli Panduga**, **Kalimas**.

272.s: Which tribe celebrates Bhumi Panduga, held before monsoon sowing and ending with the Kommu dance?
272.x: Bhumi Panduga is a Koya festival of the Godavari agency.

272.s: During Seethala Panduga, against which of the following do the Lambadis worship Seethala Mata as a guard?
272.x: Seethala Mata is believed to guard against smallpox.

272.s: By what other name is Heli Panduga, the Lambadi festival for newborn sons, known?
272.x: Heli Panduga is also called Jari Gundu and features the Jojer Nrutyam.

272.s: What is the name of the dance performed by the tribes of Araku Valley?
272.x: Tribes of the Araku Valley such as Bagata, Kondu and Valmiki perform the Dhimsa dance.

272.s:
Consider the following statements about the Dhimsa dance:
1. Its origin is traced to Koraput.
2. It is danced in circles with hands on one another's shoulders.
3. It is performed by groups of about 50-60 women.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
272.x: Dhimsa originated in Koraput and is danced in circles with hands on the shoulders; the groups are of about 15-20 women, not 50-60.

272.s:
Consider the following pairs (dance – community):
1. Kommu – Koya
2. Gussadi – Lambada
3. Lambadi dance – Lambada/Sugali women
Which of the above pairs are correctly matched?
272.x: Kommu is the Koya dance and the Lambadi dance is by Lambada/Sugali women; Gussadi is a Gond dance.
xa: ⚠ **Gussadi** = **Gond**; **Kommu** = **Koya**.
**Dhimsa**: **Bagata, Gadaba, Kondadora, Poraja, Valmiki**.
Lambadi festival with dance: **Heli Panduga** with **Jojer Nrutyam**.

272.s: The Dhimsa dance of the Andhra agency is chiefly performed by which of the following tribes?
o: Bagata, Gadaba, Kondadora, Poraja and Valmiki
272.x: Dhimsa is danced by the Bagata, Gadaba, Kondadora, Poraja and Valmiki (other sources add Savara, Jatapu, Khond and Kotia). The Gond perform Gussadi; Lambada/Sugali women perform the Lambadi dance; the Koya perform the Kommu (bison-horn) dance.
272.tq: Dhimsa = agency tribes (Bagata, Gadaba...); Gussadi = Gond; Kommu = Koya.
xs: **Dhimsa** is danced by the **Bagata, Gadaba, Kondadora, Poraja and Valmiki** — option **(1)**.
**Gond** = **Gussadi**; **Lambada/Sugali** = **Lambadi** dance; **Koya** = **Kommu** dance.
xa: CDCA adds **Savara, Jatapu**; APP adds **Khond, Kotia**.
Region: **ASR** and **Parvathipuram Manyam**; origin **Koraput**.
Instruments: **dappu, tudumu, mori, kidgi, gilka, jodukommulu**.

272.s: Where was the Guinness World Record for the largest Dhimsa dance (July 2026) set?
o: Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport, Bhogapuram
272.x: Over 13,000 tribal women and girl students danced at the Bhogapuram airport in Vizianagaram; the certificate went to the AP Tribal Welfare Department.
xa: Dhimsa: **15-20 women** per circle, hands on shoulders.
**World Adivasi Day** festival: **Tummalapalli Kalakshetram, Vijayawada** (**11 Aug 2026**).
Dhimsa origin traced to **Koraput**.

272.s: What is the headgear of Kommu dancers of the Koya tribe made of?
272.x: Kommu is the Koya dance with bison-horn headgear.

272.s: Which tribe performs the Gussadi dance?
272.x: Gussadi is a dance of the Gond tribe (Telangana side), not of the Lambada.

272.x: Savara and Gadaba are Munda languages; Koya and Gondi are Dravidian.

272.x: Savara is the only AP tribal language with a script.

272.s: Which of the following is a Munda language?
272.x: Gadaba is Munda; Gondi, Kolami and Koya are Dravidian.

272.x: Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa Rebellion in the Eastern Ghats from 1922 to 1924.
